original.title: net/http: deflake HTTP/3 tests
original.body:
We recently enabled net/http tests for our internal x/net/internal/http3 implementation in https://go.dev/cl/765320. Unfortunately, the tests end up being flaky.

The flakes seem to be mostly coming from the following issues, in order of most to least prevalent (though there might be more):

1. QUIC connections are not shutdown fast enough during test cleanup, causing them to be detected as goroutine leaks.
2. x/net/quic has a race condition where its output buffer are written to without locks (synchronously and intentionally, for optimization), but may be asynchronously written when the QUIC stream receives a `STOP_SENDING` frame.
3. Similar to 2., but for input buffer, with data race between reading and closing the stream.
4. Handshake timeout for unknown reasons when trying to establish TLS connection.

The HTTP/3 tests have therefore been temporarily disabled for now (https://go.dev/cl/766740). This is a bug to track the actual fix and to dedupe the many watchflake issues that were opened.

original.title: cmd/go: change `go mod init` default go directive to 1.(N-n).0
original.body:
This is a feature request for the default behavior of the `go mod init` command ([doc](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Initialize_new_module_in_current_directory), [ref](https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-init)).

## Background

This command creates a go.mod file for a new module, initialized with two directives: `module` and `go`. The module path, a part of the `module` directive, is provided explicitly to `go mod init` via an argument in many cases. The version used in the `go` directive is not explicitly specified by the user, and so its value is currently inferred from the currently selected version of the Go toolchain. For example:

```sh
$ cd $(mktemp -d)
$ go mod init example.com  # using go version go1.25rc2
go: creating new go.mod: module example.com
$ cat go.mod
module example.com

go 1.25rc2
```

The go command has no good way of knowing what value of the `go` directive the user intends to use in the module being created eventually, so when picking an initial value for it, it uses a simple heuristic: "the latest version supported by this toolchain".

This behavior has a property of being simple, predictable, and importantly, it can work while completely offline (i.e., no internet connection required).

## Feature Request

I suggest changing the initial default version to the following behavior:

- if the current toolchain version is a stable version of Go 1.N.M, default to `go 1.(N-1).0`
- if the current toolchain version is a pre-release version of Go 1.N (Release Candidate M) or a development version of Go 1.N, default to `go 1.(N-2).0`

Using version types as defined [here](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain#version). This behavior maintains the property of being able to work offline. While more complex and less predictable, it is still fairly simple.

Examples of the new behavior:

```sh
$ cd $(mktemp -d)
$ go mod init example.com  # using go version go1.25rc2
go: creating new go.mod: module example.com
$ cat go.mod
module example.com

go 1.23.0

$ cd $(mktemp -d)

original.title: x/tools/gopls: add `shadowing` semantic token modifier
original.body: #75342 made me think that I so often catch shadow bugs early, because i have the shadow analyzer enabled, that it would be nice to have some better way to expose such functionality to users, such that these are not warnings, but as a hint. This is not only about variable naming bugs, but I often get frustrated that `url.` does not give any autocomplete only to realize that I have declared an `url` variable. It would be nice to have a way to give attention to some parts of code. My proposition is we add a `shadowing` semantic token modifier, that is returned to the editor, when an identifier causes other identifier, from outer scope(s), to be shadowed. Example: It requires (at least in nvim) some special configuration: ```lua vim.api.nvim_set_hl(0, '@lsp.mod.shadowing', { bold=true, underline=true }) ``` CC @adonovan

original.title: x/pkgsite: swap ?GOOS=darwin to arm64?
original.body:
By default, pkgsite renders for linux-amd64, but offers a few "popular" alternative GOOS/GOARCH combinations, currently linux/amd64, windows/amd64, darwin/amd64, and js/wasm.

I believe we have previously been hesitant to add more configurations due to additional processing cost, but I wonder if we should replace darwin/amd64 with darwin/arm64, given that the former is only declining in use due to no new darwin/amd64.

A one-off non-scientific look at https://storage.googleapis.com/prod-telemetry-merged/2025-03-15.json has ~90% of darwin reports from darwin/arm64.

duplicate.title: archive/tar: base-256 UID/GID values silently truncate on 32-bit platforms
duplicate.body:
### Go version

Reproduced with go1.24.7 (GOARCH=386). The same code is unchanged on master (dfe2e7bfb4).

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
Linux, GOARCH=386 (the bug only shows on platforms where int is 32 bits).
```

### What did you do?

Read a tar header whose uid (or gid) field uses the GNU base-256 encoding with a value outside the 32-bit `int` range, for example uid = 4294967296 (2^32).

In `readHeader` (src/archive/tar/reader.go), the V7 uid/gid fields are parsed with `parseNumeric`, which returns an `int64`, and then converted with `int(...)` without a range check:

```
hdr.Uid = int(p.parseNumeric(v7.uid()))
hdr.Gid = int(p.parseNumeric(v7.gid()))
```

The same truncation was fixed for PAX `uid`/`gid` records in [CL 822060](https://go.dev/cl/822060) (#81129), but the base-256 path in `readHeader` was not covered.

Minimal reproduction, as a test in package `tar` (run with `GOARCH=386 go test -run TestReadHeaderBase256IDOverflow archive/tar`):

```
var blk block
var f formatter
v7 := blk.toV7()
copy(v7.name(), "file")
v7.typeFlag()[0] = TypeReg
f.formatOctal(v7.mode(), 0644)
f.formatNumeric(v7.uid(), 1<<32) // encoded as base-256
f.formatOctal(v7.size(), 0)
f.formatOctal(v7.modTime(), 0)
blk.setFormat(FormatGNU)
hdr, err := NewReader(bytes.NewReader(append(blk[:], make([]byte, 2*blockSize)...))).Next()
```

### What did you see happen?

On `GOARCH=386`, `Next()` returns no error and `hdr.Uid == 0`. The encoded owner (4294967296) is silently replaced by 0 (root). Values such as 2^31 wrap to negative.

### What did you expect to see?

`Next()` should return `ErrHeader`, consistent with the PAX uid/gid handling after [CL 822060](https://go.dev/cl/822060).

### Notes

This was first reported privately to [security@golang.org](mailto:security@golang.org); the security team classified it as a regular bug and suggested filing it here. I have a fix with a test ready to send as a CL.

original.title: archive/tar: UID/GID overflow check added to mergePAX is missing on the USTAR/v7 path
original.body:
### Go version

`master` (verified at the commit that added the `mergePAX` bounds check, cc740a9f1b)

### What did you do?

[CL 822060](https://go.dev/cl/822060) / #81130 (fixes #81129) added a bounds check to `mergePAX`, because `paxUid`/`paxGid` are
parsed as `int64` and then cast to platform `int`, silently truncating on 32-bit.

The same narrowing exists on the plain USTAR/v7 header path and was not changed:

[https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/archive/tar/reader.go#L394-L395](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/archive/tar/reader.go#L394-L395)

```go
hdr.Uid = int(p.parseNumeric(v7.uid()))
hdr.Gid = int(p.parseNumeric(v7.gid()))
```

It is reachable because `parseNumeric` accepts GNU **base-256** numeric fields — when `b[0]&0x80` is
set the remaining bytes are a two's-complement big-endian integer — and rejects only values that
overflow `int64`:

```go
if (x >> 56) > 0 { p.err = ErrHeader; return 0 }
...
if (x >> 63) > 0 { p.err = ErrHeader; return 0 }
```

So an 8-byte `uid` field can carry `2^32`, well above 32-bit `int`. Plain octal cannot (7 digits ⇒
max 2097151), which may be why this field looked safe.

Reproducer — builds a valid USTAR header (correct checksum) whose `uid` field is base-256 `2^32`,
then parses it with `archive/tar`:

```go
package main

import (
	"archive/tar"
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"strconv"
)

func base256(v uint64, n int) []byte {
	b := make([]byte, n)
	for i := n - 1; i >= 1; i-- {
		b[i] = byte(v)
		v >>= 8
	}
	b[0] = 0x80 // flag bit, value bits zero
	return b
}

func main() {
	var uid uint64 = 1 << 32

	h := make([]byte, 512)
	copy(h[0:], "poc.txt")
	copy(h[100:], "0000644\x00")
	copy(h[108:], base256(uid, 8)) // uid, base-256
	copy(h[116:], "0000000\x00")
	copy(h[124:], "00000000000\x00")
	copy(h[136:], "00000000000\x00")
	h[156] = '0'
	copy(h[257:], "ustar\x0000")
	for i := 148; i < 156; i++ {
		h[i] = ' '
	}
	sum := 0
	for _, c := range h {
		sum += int(c)
	}
	copy(h[148:], fmt.Sprintf("%06o\x00 ", sum))

	va

original.title: x/crypto/ocsp: ParseResponse makes incorrect choices about response and issuer verification
original.body:
`x/crypto/ocsp` makes an incorrect assumption about the contents of the `BasicOCSPResponse`'s `certs` field and has a broken API as a result.

---

Per [RFC 6960 Section 4.2.1 ASN.1 Specification of the OCSP Response](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6960#section-4.2.1): 

>  The responder MAY include certificates in
>  the `certs` field of `BasicOCSPResponse` that help the OCSP client verify
>  the responder's signature.  If no certificates are included, then
>  `certs` SHOULD be absent.

Notably, the RFC makes no assertions about the contents of these certificates, whether they are strictly delegated OCSP issuers (as discussed in [another Go issue](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/40017) or whether they can include or not include intermediate CAs necessary to tie the OCSP responder's cert back to a concrete root.

However, `x/crypto/ocsp`'s `ParseResponse` and `ParseResponseForCertificate` incorrectly assume that any certificates included in the response are a delegated OCSP signer and its chain, assuming the delegated OCSP signer is the first certificate. This is not guaranteed by the RFC and is not assumed by other OCSP libraries. Go is unique and non-conformant in this regard.

In particular, _if_ the caller passes an `issuer` parameter value, Go [incorrectly assumes](https://github.com/golang/crypto/blob/1faeef9713563c936e077b84e4c3a0f3cac0fbe4/ocsp/ocsp.go#L569-L579) that this issuer _must_ have either directly issued the OCSP response or issued the first certificate in the `BasicOCSPResponse`'s `certs` field. 

This has no basis in the RFC.

Further, and more risky is the beavhior around `issuer=nil`: here, while the `BasicOCSPResponse`'s `certs` field is used to verify the signature, no grounding to a trusted certificate. This is _only_ safe over a secure transport for OCSP requests/responses and the docs make no mention of this. (cc @golang/security and @rolandshoemaker).

---

duplicate.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: unwrap variadic literal in empty-body discard
duplicate.body:
This forks off related work from #63352 (empty-body reduction). There is an existing TODO in that strategy:

> if args is the []T{a1, ..., an} literal synthesized during variadic simplification, consider unwrapping it to its (pure) elements.

## Problem

When reducing a call to an empty variadic function, variadic simplification first synthesizes a `[]T{a1, ..., an}` literal. The empty-body discard then keeps that temporary slice:

```go
func f(...T) {}
f(a, b, c)
→ _ = []T{a, b, c}
```

The slice is unnecessary: the elements only need to be evaluated for effects.

## Proposed approach

When discarding a call to an empty function:

1. Detect the `[]T{a1, ..., an}` literal synthesized during variadic simplification.
2. Unwrap it and discard the elements with a parallel blank assignment: `_, _, _ = a, b, c`.
3. Do not keep the temporary slice.

CL: https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/tools/+/814401

original.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: unwrap variadic literal in empty-body discard
original.body:
This forks off related work from #63352 (empty-body reduction). There is an existing TODO in that strategy:

> if args is the []T{a1, ..., an} literal synthesized during variadic simplification, consider unwrapping it to its (pure) elements.

## Problem

A call to an empty variadic function is first rewritten as a single slice argument. The empty-body discard then keeps that temporary slice just to evaluate the elements:

```go
func empty(...any) {}
empty(-1, ch, len(""), g(), <-ch)
→ _ = []any{-1, ch, len(""), g(), <-ch}
```

The slice is never read. The elements only need to be evaluated for effects. A parallel blank assignment does that without allocating a composite literal.

## Proposed approach

In the empty-body discard, after variadic simplification:

1. If the sole remaining argument is the `[]T{a1, ..., an}` composite literal from a variadic parameter, unwrap it.
2. Discard the elements with a parallel blank assignment: `_, _, _ = a1, a2, a3`.
3. If the literal has no elements, delete the statement (`empty()` → empty stmt).
4. Non-variadic / non-literal remaining args stay as `_ = args`.

```go
empty(-1, ch, len(""), g(), <-ch)
→ _, _, _, _, _ = -1, ch, len(""), g(), <-ch

empty()
→ /* deleted */
```

There is an existing TODO next to that strategy:

> TODO: discard go or defer statements as well.

## Problem

Inlining `go f()` or `defer f()` when `f` has an empty body currently keeps the `go`/`defer` wrapper. The scheduled call is a no-op; only argument evaluation (if any) has effects.

## Proposed approach

Extend the empty-body strategy to `GoStmt` and `DeferStmt`:

1. Drop the `go`/`defer` wrapper.
2. Keep argument evaluation only for effects (`_, _ = args`, or delete the statement entirely when there are no remaining args).

original.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: discard go/defer of empty functions
original.body:
This forks off related work from #63352 (empty-body reduction). The empty-body strategy already deletes a call to a function with an empty body, but `callStmt` is nil when the call is the argument of `go` or `defer`. There is an existing TODO next to that strategy:

> TODO: discard go or defer statements as well.

## Problem

`go` and `defer` evaluate arguments in the calling goroutine, then schedule the call. If the callee body is empty, that scheduled call is a no-op, but inlining currently keeps the wrapper:

```go
func f() {}
go f()
→ go func() {}()     // or the call is left alone

func f(x int) {}
defer f(recover().(int))
→ defer still wraps a no-op; recover is not evaluated as a plain statement
```

Only argument evaluation (if any) has effects. The `go`/`defer` itself does not.

## Proposed approach

Extend the existing empty-body discard to `GoStmt` and `DeferStmt` when the call is exactly `parent.Call`:

1. Drop the `go`/`defer` wrapper (replace the whole statement, not just the call).
2. If remaining arguments have effects, keep `_ = args` (same as a plain empty-body call).
3. If there are no remaining arguments, delete the statement entirely.
4. Non-empty callees stay on the existing path (literalize under `go`/`defer`).

```go
go f()                          // empty, no args
→ /* deleted */

defer f()                       // empty, no args
→ /* deleted */

go f(recover().(int))           // empty, arg effects
→ _ = recover().(int)

go f()                          // non-empty body
→ go func() { println("work") }()
```

CL: https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/tools/+/814523

duplicate.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: wrap void calls out of if/for/switch init
duplicate.body:
This forks off one item from #63352:

> Translate `if f(); cond { ... }` to `{ fbody; if cond { ... } }` when the inlining of f() is not a simple expression.

## Problem

`callStmt(..., unrestricted)` returns nil when a void call appears as `IfStmt.Init`, `ForStmt.Init`, or `SwitchStmt.Init`. Those are restricted statement contexts, so the inliner falls back to literalization:

```go
if f(); cond { ... }
→ if func() { fbody }(); cond { ... }
```

The existing TODO in `callStmt` already describes wrapping the if/for/switch in a block instead. `ForStmt.Post` must stay restricted.

## Proposed approach

When inlining a void call used as the Init of an if, for, or switch:

1. Detect that restricted Init context.
2. Lift the callee body into a surrounding block and clear the Init: `{ fbody; if cond { ... } }`.
3. Leave `ForStmt.Post` alone. Otherwise keep the existing literalization fallback.

> choose better local names for renaming imports

## Problem

When `findNewLocalName` cannot reuse the callee's local name or the declared package name, it falls back immediately to a numeric suffix (`path0`, `format3`). Those names are valid but low-quality.

original.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: prefer pathpkg-style local import names
original.body:
This forks off one item from #63352:

> choose better local names for renaming imports

#74965 discussed this and was closed after the callee-alias strategy landed (CL 712981). This issue is the remaining work: better fallbacks after the callee alias and the declared package name are unavailable.

## Problem

When `findNewLocalName` cannot reuse the callee's local name or the declared package name, it falls back immediately to a numeric suffix:

```go
// caller already uses the name "path"
path.Dir(g())
→ import path0 "testdata/path"
   path0.Split(...)
```

`path0` is unique but not idiomatic. The usual Go style, including in this repo, is `pathpkg "path"` or a preceding path segment (`internalastutil`).

## Proposed approach

After trying the callee alias and `pkgName`, try more names before a numeric suffix. A name is available if it is a non-`init` identifier and is not shadowed in the caller, not already added, and not in the shadow map:

1. `pkgName + "pkg"` (e.g. `path` → `pathpkg`).
2. Preceding path segment + `pkgName` when that segment is an identifier (e.g. `testdata/path` → `testdatapath`, `internal/astutil` → `internalastutil`).
3. Only then `pkgName` + `0`, `1`, … If `pkgName` itself is not a legal identifier, use `pkg` as the numeric base.

```go
// "path" is taken
path.Dir(g())
→ import pathpkg "testdata/path"

// "path" and "pathpkg" are both taken
→ import testdatapath "testdata/path"
```

No camel case (package names stay lowercase, as adonovan asked on #74965). The callee alias from CL 712981 stays first.

duplicate.body:
This forks off one item from #63352:

> implement parameterless call to { stmt; return expr } from one of these contexts:
>
>         //    x, y     = f()
>         //    x, y    := f()
>         //    var x, y = f()

## Problem

A parameterless call whose body is statements followed by a single return is currently literalized when it appears as the RHS of an assignment or var declaration:

```go
x, y = f()
→ x, y = func() (T1, T2) { stmts; return expr }()
```

Literalization is unnecessary: the call is already in statement context, so the callee statements can be emitted before assigning the return expression.

## Proposed approach

Add a reduction strategy that:

1. Applies only to parameterless callees whose body is `{ stmts; return expr }` (a single return).
2. In `=`, `:=`, and `var` contexts, keeps the callee statements in an inner block and then assigns the return expression to the LHS, so those statements cannot shadow the assignment targets.
3. Otherwise keeps the existing literalization fallback.

original.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: inline parameterless {stmts; return} calls in assign context
original.body:
This forks off one item from #63352:

> implement parameterless call to { stmt; return expr } from one of these contexts:
>
>         //    x, y     = f()
>         //    x, y    := f()
>         //    var x, y = f()

## Problem

A parameterless call whose body is statements followed by a single return is currently literalized when it is the sole RHS of an assignment or var declaration:

```go
func f() (int, int) { println("work"); return 1, 2 }

x, y = f()
→ x, y = func() (int, int) { println("work"); return 1, 2 }()
```

Literalization is unnecessary: the call is already a statement. The callee statements can run first, then the return operands can be assigned to the LHS.

adonovan's original sketch (`var (x T1, y T2); { stmts; x, y = expr }`) is heavier than needed. We already have `assignStmts` for converting a return into `=`, `:=`, or `var`.

## Proposed approach

Add a dedicated assign-context strategy:

1. Match only a parameterless callee whose body is `{ stmts; return exprs }` (exactly one return, and it is the last statement). No binding decl, no `defer`, no label conflict.
2. In `x, y = f()` or `x, y := f()` (sole RHS, unrestricted statement parent): keep `stmts` in an **inner** block so callee locals cannot shadow the assignment LHS, then assign the return operands via `assignStmts`.
3. In `var x, y = f()` (single ValueSpec): same, lowered to `x, y := exprs`. For `:=` / `var`, elide the **outer** braces so the definition stays in the caller scope.
4. Otherwise keep literalization: `defer` in the callee, multiple returns, return not last, mixed RHS (`x, z = f(), 0`), or a needed binding decl.

```go
var x, y int
x, y = f()
→
var x, y int
{
	println("work")
}
x, y = 1, 2

x, y := f()
→
{
	println("work")
}
x, y := 1, 2

// callee local must not steal the caller's x
var x int
x = f()   // callee: x := 1; println(x); return 2
→
var x int
{
	x := 1
	println(x)
}
x = 2
```

CL: https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/tools/+/814442

This forks off one item from #63352:

> simplify "binding decl" to use `param := arg` when it's not necessary to state the type.

## Problem

`createBindingDecl` currently always emits a typed `var` declaration:

```go
var param T = arg
```

even when the argument's type already matches the parameter type. The extra type is redundant and less natural than a short declaration.

## Proposed approach

When building a binding declaration:

1. Omit the explicit type and use `param := arg` when the argument type already matches the parameter type.
2. Keep a typed `var` declaration when a conversion is required.
3. Use `_ = arg` for blank-only bindings instead of `var _ T = arg`.

original.title: x/tools/internal/refactor/inline: simplify binding decls to param := arg when types are redundant
original.body:
This forks off one item from #63352:

> simplify "binding decl" to use `param := arg` when it's not necessary to state the type.

## Problem

`createBindingDecl` always emits a typed `var` declaration, even when the argument type already matches the parameter type:

```go
func f(s string) { defer println(); println(s) }
f("hi")
→ func() { var s string = "hi"; defer println(); println(s) }()
```

The explicit type is redundant. A short declaration is the usual Go form, and it also avoids some shadowing: if an earlier parameter is named `int`, a later `var z int = arg` cannot be emitted, but `z := arg` can.

Blank-only bindings are worse still: `var _ int = z` is not idiomatic.

## Proposed approach

When building the binding declaration, compare `types.Default(arg.Type)` with the parameter type (`types.Default` so an untyped constant gets its default type; `arg.constant` is unreliable because it may still carry the parameter type from the original call, e.g. untyped `1` passed to `float64`):

1. If every argument in a parameter group already has the parameter type, omit the type and emit `param := arg` (or `p0, p1 := a0, a1`).
2. If any argument needs a conversion, keep a typed `var` spec for that group:
   `var x any = g()`.
3. If every bound name is `_`, emit `_ = arg` instead of `:=` (`:=` needs at least one new non-blank name).
4. Named result variables still use a typed `var` decl (they have no initializer).

```go
f("hi")
→ func() { s := "hi"; defer println(); println(s) }()

f(g())  // g() int, param any
→ func() { var x any = g(); ... }()

f(z)    // unused param
→ _ = z
```

CL: https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/tools/+/814441

`go1.26.5` (toolchain host `darwin/arm64`, cross-compiling and executing on `linux/amd64`), `GOEXPERIMENT=simd`.

```go
package main

import "simd/archsimd"

//go:noinline
func chains(x []float32, n int) archsimd.Float32x16 {
	v := archsimd.LoadFloat32x16Slice(x)
	a0 := archsimd.LoadFloat32x16Slice(x[0:])
	a1 := archsimd.LoadFloat32x16Slice(x[16:])
	// ... aN-1
	for k := 0; k < n; k++ {
		a0 = v.MulAdd(v, a0)
		a1 = v.MulAdd(v, a1)
		// ... aN-1
	}
	s := a0
	s = s.Add(a1)
	// ... aN-1
	return s
}

func main() {
	x := make([]float32, 1024)
	_ = chains(x, 3)
}
```

(Accumulators must be distinct named variables rather than an array element — an
array is not SROA'd here and goes to memory for an unrelated reason, cf. #79322.)

Then counted, in the steady-state loop of the `-gcflags=-S` listing, the vector
stack traffic and the set of `Z` registers named anywhere in the function.

### What did you expect to see?

AVX-512 has 32 architectural vector registers, and `_gen/AMD64Ops.go:128` declares
the operand mask used by the AVX-512 ops as 31 of them:

```go
w = buildReg("X0 X1 X2 X3 X4 X5 X6 X7 X8 X9 X10 X11 X12 X13 X14 X16 X17 X18 X19 X20 X21 X22 X23 X24 X25 X26 X27 X28 X29 X30 X31")
```

`VFMADD213PS512` and friends use the `w31` shape built from it, so the op
definitions say Z16–Z31 are legal operands. I expected the frontier — the largest
`N` with no spilling — to be about 29 (31 registers, minus the shared multiplicand,
minus one scratch), and I expected to see registers above Z15 in the listing.

### What did you see instead?

The frontier is **13**, and **no register above Z14 is ever named**, in any of the
functions, at any `N`:

| N (accumulators) | insns in loop | vector stack refs per iteration | register copies |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | 43 | **0** | 27 |
| 14

original.body:
We have had four CI jobs fail in the past week due to `sum.golang.org` reporting 500 internal server errors as well as an unexpected EOF.

* https://github.com/cue-lang/cuelang.org/actions/runs/11405713492/job/31737794702
* https://github.com/cue-lang/cuelang.org/actions/runs/11406304337/job/31739760236
* https://github.com/cue-lang/cuelang.org/actions/runs/11494340883/job/31991655336
* https://github.com/cue-lang/cuelang.org/actions/runs/11514929154/job/32054554147

The two types of errors we have seen look like:

> go: cuelang.org/go@v0.11.0-alpha.3.0.20241018144220-537f744a9cc7: verifying go.mod: cuelang.org/go@v0.11.0-alpha.3.0.20241018144220-537f744a9cc7/go.mod: reading https://sum.golang.org/lookup/cuelang.org/go@v0.11.0-alpha.3.0.20241018144220-537f744a9cc7: 500 Internal Server Error

> go: cuelang.org/go@v0.10.1: verifying module: cuelang.org/go@v0.10.1: Get "https://sum.golang.org/lookup/cuelang.org/go@v0.10.1": EOF

These CI jobs are doing what is effectively:

```
go mod init
go get cuelang.org/go@${commitRef}
```

where `${commitRef}` is a commit hash which was just pushed to master.

We are aware that `proxy.golang.org` and `sum.golang.org` may respond with status codes like 404 for the first fifteen to thirty minutes as they discover the new version (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/49916#issuecomment-984839295), but I still assume that the 500 and EOF errors are unexpected and should be fixed.

Moreover, we do dozens of these runs per week, and only very few fail, so `sum.golang.org` often answers these requests correctly without any issue.

duplicate.title: proposal: bytes: export the readSlice method
duplicate.body:
### Proposal Details

`readSlice` is an unexported method of `bytes.Buffer`, seen here
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/c122d7e6c50f8f1950a99b8e7b2b36e8a54cffce/src/bytes/buffer.go#L456-L468
Users can call `readSlice` through either the `ReadBytes` or `ReadString` methods, but both of these make copies of the data in the buffer, rather than returning a slice of the internal buffer itself.

The slice returned by `readSlice` is only valid until the next call to a method that modifies the buffer. This could cause issues if used improperly, but this is already  true for the `Bytes`, `AvailableBuffer`, `Next`, and `Peek` methods, and is documented accordingly. See here:
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/c122d7e6c50f8f1950a99b8e7b2b36e8a54cffce/src/bytes/buffer.go#L55-L60
`bufio.Reader` also includes a `ReadSlice` method that behaves the same way and is exported, see https://pkg.go.dev/bufio@go1.26.5#Reader.ReadSlice

Using the source code as a basis I created my own version of the `readSlice` method, which looks like this
```go
func ReadSlice(b *bytes.Buffer, delim byte) (line []byte, err error) {
	buf := b.Bytes()
	i := bytes.IndexByte(buf, delim)
	end := i + 1
	if i < 0 {
		end = len(buf)
		err = io.EOF
	}
	line = buf[:end]
	b.Next(end)
	return line, err
}
```

I wrote a program to benchmark this function compared to `Buffer.ReadBytes`, which is available as a gist [here](https://gist.github.com/GeorgeTR1/2361c6ce2b563516a9ed4d4c338c489e). I would have linked it on the playground, but it times out without running. Running it on my machine returned the following results:
```
>go run bytesBench.go
using Buffer.ReadBytes
  749185              1409 ns/op
    1144 B/op         27 allocs/op
using custom ReadSlice function
 3100702               384.8 ns/op
       0 B/op          0 allocs/op
```
The version that avoided copying didn't allocate any memory and ran over 3 times faster, which I would consider quite significant.

original.title: bytes: buffer.readSlice is not exported
original.body:
Currently, `readSlice` method in `bytes.Buffer` is private, which means there is no easy way to read the buffer by delimiter without needlessly allocating another slice.

Since it is already there, and [bufio package has the same method exported](https://golang.org/pkg/bufio/#Reader.ReadSlice), I propose making this method exported in the `bytes` package as well (with proper warnings about its usage in the comments, the same way `bufio` does it).

I can submit a patch, but since I'm not sure whether these kind of changes are acceptable (it is non-breaking change, right?), I'd rather ask first.

original.title: encoding/json: JSONv2 baseline changes SyntaxError and UnmarshalTypeError offsets
original.body:
Hi 👋🏻 

While testing [k6](https://github.com/grafana/k6) against Go tip, we noticed failures that appear to be caused by changed `encoding/json` error offsets after JSONv2 became the baseline implementation.

We are not sure whether this offset change is intended behavior with JSONv2, or whether this is an unexpected compatibility issue in the v1 `encoding/json` API.

The first Go commit where we observe the behavior is: https://github.com/golang/go/commit/e62d3e6e897175a07aa44a7b2c7f99700072f22f

That commit says:

> By JSONv2 becoming baseline, the v1 "encoding/json" will be implemented under-the-hood using v2, while preserving v1 semantics.

Given that, we wanted to ask whether the changed offsets below are expected.

  ### Reproducer

```go
  package main

  import (
        "encoding/json"
        "fmt"
  )

  func main() {
        var v any
        err := json.Unmarshal([]byte("{\n  \"key\": treu\n}"), &v)
        if se, ok := err.(*json.SyntaxError); ok {
                fmt.Printf("SyntaxError.Offset = %d, error = %v\n", se.Offset, se)
        }

        type options struct {
                Tags map[string]string `json:"tags"`
        }
        var opts options
        err = json.Unmarshal([]byte("{\"tags\": []}"), &opts)
        if ute, ok := err.(*json.UnmarshalTypeError); ok {
                fmt.Printf("UnmarshalTypeError.Offset = %d, error = %v\n", ute.Offset, ute)
        }
  }
```

  ### Observed

  With Go tip default JSONv2 baseline:

```go
SyntaxError.Offset = 13
UnmarshalTypeError.Offset = 9
```

With GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2, or older Go without JSONv2 baseline:

```go
SyntaxError.Offset = 14
UnmarshalTypeError.Offset = 10
```



### Impact

[k6](https://github.com/grafana/k6) continuously tests against the go tip and uses these offsets to produce user-facing JSON parse diagnostics. The changed offsets make our diagnostics point one character earlier than before, and caused our Go tip CI to fail:

https://github.com/grafana/k6/actions/runs/2644684

duplicate.title: x/pkgsite: support offline search in local module cache
duplicate.body:
**What is the problem?**
When running the `pkgsite` server locally in offline mode using the module cache (e.g., `pkgsite -cache`), users can view documentation for cached modules if they know and enter the exact URL. However, the search functionality currently does not work for cached modules. The local `FetchDataSource` defaults to `internal.NoSearch` because `modCacheModuleGetter` does not implement the `SearchableModuleGetter` interface.

This creates friction for offline development, as users must memorize exact module paths instead of being able to search their local cache.

**What is the proposed solution?**
Implement the `Search` method on `modCacheModuleGetter` in `internal/fetch/getters.go` so that the local `FetchDataSource` can route search queries to the local module cache.

To keep the search fast and responsive without requiring a persistent database or heavy AST parsing on the fly, the implementation can perform a shallow search:

1. Scan the `GOMODCACHE/cache/download` directory structure.
2. Identify valid cached modules by looking for `@v` directories that contain a `.zip` file (this filters out "ghost" modules where the `go` toolchain only downloaded the `.mod` and `.info` files for graph resolution).
3. Extract the module path using `module.UnescapePath` and score it using `pkgsite`'s existing `fuzzy.NewSymbolMatcher`.
4. Return the matching module roots as `internal.SearchResult`s.

**Next Steps**
I have a working local implementation of this fast/shallow search approach and am currently running the tests via `./all.bash`. I will submit a Gerrit CL shortly.

original.title: cmd/compile: missing escape analysis on generic func impls
original.body:
Here is a simple program in two packages, checked into rsc.io/tmp/escbug.

```
package p

import (
	"runtime"

	"rsc.io/tmp/escbug/q"
)

func P() {
	var buf [24]byte
	runtime.KeepAlive(q.Q(buf[:0], 1))
}
```

```
package q

func nop(x int) int { return x }

func Q(dst []byte, x int64) []byte {
	return q(dst, x)
}

func q[T int32 | int64](dst []byte, x T) []byte {
	return append(dst, byte(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(nop(int(x))))))))))))))))))))))))
}
```

p.P calls q.Q with a stack buffer, which the compiler incorrectly promotes to a heap allocation.

q.Q calls q.q, which returns the result of appending to the buffer. The result of the analysis should be that the argument dst leaks to the result but not to the heap. And in fact if you build this, you do get that result when analyzing q.q and q.Q:

triage.title: go/types: Interface.Method and ExplicitMethod are not ordered by Id, contra docs
triage.body:
(Found in passing.)

The docs for types.Interface.Method say "The methods are ordered by their unique Id"; so do those for ExplicitMethod. But since https://go.dev/cl/461677 they're actually sorted with exported names before unexported ones. They differ when an interface has unexported methods from more than one package, which happens when it embeds an interface from another package:

```go
package q

type I interface{ a() }
```

```go
package p

import "q"

type J interface {
	q.I
	b()
}
```

Program (type-checks both packages and prints the methods of `J`):

```go
iface := J.Underlying().(*types.Interface)
for i := range iface.NumMethods() {
	fmt.Println(iface.Method(i).Id())
}
mset := types.NewMethodSet(J)
for i := range mset.Len() {
	fmt.Println(mset.At(i).Obj().Id())
}
```

Prints:
```
Interface.Method order:
	q.a
	p.b
MethodSet order:
	p.b
	q.a
```

`Interface.Method` yields `q.a` before `p.b`, although `"p.b" < "q.a"`.
`MethodSet`, whose documentation also promises Id order, does sort by Id.

They can also differ for exported versus unexported names, when a package path
sorts before an exported name (e.g. path `"M"`, methods `Z` and `a`: Id order is
`M.a`, `Z`, but `Interface.Method` yields `Z` first). That's rare in practice.

I'm not sure whether it's safe the order back; we may need to just document the actual order.

triage.title: x/website: document GOAUTH for private module proxies
triage.body:
The [private module proxy authentication section](https://go.dev/ref/mod#private-module-proxy-auth)
currently says that the `go` command supports HTTP Basic authentication and
documents credentials supplied through `.netrc` or directly in `GOPROXY`.

Since Go 1.24, the `GOAUTH` environment variable also applies to HTTPS module
mirror interactions. In addition to its default `netrc` mode, it can use Git
credential helpers or invoke a custom command that returns arbitrary HTTP
headers for HTTPS URL prefixes.

This is relevant to private module proxies that use Bearer tokens, short-lived
credentials, external credential helpers, or different credentials for paths
on the same host. Those configurations are not discoverable from the current
module reference, even though `GOAUTH` is the supported mechanism for them.

The section could be updated to:

- distinguish Basic authentication through `.netrc` or URL userinfo from the
  more general headers supported by `GOAUTH`;
- mention that custom commands can return headers for HTTPS URL prefixes;
- explain that URL-prefix matching allows path-scoped credentials;
- link to `go help goauth` for the complete command protocol;
- state that credentials obtained through `GOAUTH` are only applied to HTTPS
  requests.

This would be a documentation-only change. The implementation and [Go 1.24
release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.24#go-command) already describe
`GOAUTH`; the gap is in the task-oriented module proxy reference.

Related implementation issues: #26232, #71889, and #80597.

triage.title: encoding/json/v2: possibly clarify retention prohibitions in documentation
triage.body:
### General suggestion

The current json/v2 documentation lists some prohibitions regarding retaining references to slices or other memory.

Before json/v2 goes out the door, I wonder if it would be worthwhile to do a quick sweep to see if there should be any clarification or additional prohibitions laid out.

### Some current examples

For example, the [Unmarshaler](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json/v2@master#Unmarshaler) interface documentation currently says:

```
Implementations must not retain or mutate the input []byte.
```

The [UnmarshalFunc](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json/v2@master#UnmarshalFunc) documentation I think incorporates that by reference ("Implementations must follow the requirements of Unmarshaler"), but goes further and also says:

```
Implementations must not retain the value of T.
```

### Avoiding retaining destination of unmarshals

I'm particularly interested if it could or should by clearly documented that it is prohibited to retain the unmarshal method receiver or the T value supplied to an unmarshal operation after the method or function returns (or something along those lines -- I'm not trying to suggest exact language at this point).

It's probably already a bad idea for someone to retain a pointer to those? For example, if the destination is an element of a slice, the slice might have grown after the element's unmarshal completed, and the user could be pointing to a stale element in the old backing array and hence not the final element that was shallow copied during growth.

There are some things in the doc that already reference shallow copying, but I'm not sure there is currently a clear prohibition against retaining a pointer to the destination.

I'm not as deep on the latest json/v2 documentation as I probably should be, so sorry in advance if this suggestion is off base (including maybe some or all of this is already implied by a more careful read).

CC @ChrisHines @neild

triage.title: movegen documentation correction
triage.body:
### What is the URL of the page with the issue?
 
 https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/domino14/macondo/movegen
 
Documentation includes the following statement:

"It makes heavy use of the GADDAG. Implementation notes: - Is the specification in the paper a bit buggy? Basically, if I assume an anchor is the leftmost tile of a word, the way the algorithm works, it will create words blindly. For example, if I have a word FIRE on the board, and I have the letter E on my rack, and I specify F as the anchor, it will create the word EF! (Ignoring the fact that IRE is on the board) You can see this by just stepping through the algorithm. It seems that anchors can only be on the rightmost tile of a word"

The entire point of anchor squares is to reduce almost all the creation of duplicate words.  Only one anchor square is necessary to generate all the words that incorporate a word already on the board (like FIRE).  Making both the first and last letter in the word anchor squares (in the direction of the word) would generate the exact same words twice.  The implementation starts from the last tile because the GADDAG would go through all the existing letters first, eliminating many paths that would never succeed.

I could not find the email address of the author so that I could just email this explanation.

triage.title: proposal: go/doc, x/pkgsite: a //go:doc directive for author control over package documentation rendering
triage.body:
<!--
Related/adjacent issues found during research (none is a duplicate of this):
  - golang/go#69265  proposal: x/pkgsite: package tours (adds a modality; adjacent)
  - golang/go#42653  x/pkgsite: search in page is made less useful by hidden content (tangential UX)
  - golang/go#35544  proposal: cmd/doc: module documentation (OPEN, Proposal-Hold since 2019; different thing)
Source verification done against ~/src/go/go @ 7db85e388c and golang/pkgsite master.
-->

## Abstract

I propose a `//go:doc` comment directive, parsed by `go/doc`, that lets a package author control how documentation tools render the package. As the first consumer, x/pkgsite uses it to decide whether a package page renders the package doc comment, the directory README, or both. This resolves the current behavior in which pkg.go.dev renders both and duplicates every shared concept.

## Background

A package's documentation exists in two modalities:

1. Package doc comments (`doc.go` / `// Package ...`), parsed by `go/doc` and rendered by `go doc`.
2. A directory `README`, rendered by GitHub, GitLab, and x/pkgsite.

`go doc` and `go/doc` read only the doc comment. x/pkgsite renders both: it detects a README (`internal/fetch/readme.go`: any file whose base name is `README`, case-insensitive, excluding `.go`/`.vendor`, preferring `.md`/`.markdown`) and renders it below the Overview (`internal/frontend/markdown.go`: Markdown for `.md`/`.markdown`, otherwise preformatted text).

Two capabilities are missing:

1. **`go/doc` has no directive for author control over rendering.** An author cannot express intent about how a package's documentation is presented.
2. **x/pkgsite has no per-package configuration surface.** Its render behavior is fixed; there is no opt-out and no way to select a modality.

Because both capabilities are absent, a package that ships a substantive `doc.go` and a `README.md` (a common, and even encouraged pattern), a package's pkg.go.dev page has both stacked, meaning every concep

triage.title: doc: fips140 page does not specify which crypto module version is used when GODEBUG=fips140=on without GOFIPS140
triage.body:
The [FIPS 140-3 documentation](https://go.dev/doc/security/fips140) states:

> If set to `on`, FIPS 140-3 mode is enabled. This is possible even if `GOFIPS140` was not set at build time.

and later:

> Most programs should not set this option directly, and should instead use `GOFIPS140` at build time.

The document does not explain **why** `GOFIPS140` at build time is preferred, nor what actually happens to the cryptographic module version when `GODEBUG=fips140=on` is used on a binary built without `GOFIPS140`.

**The gap:** if `GODEBUG=fips140=on/only` but `GOFIPS140` does not specify a crypto module version, the `crypto/fips140.Version()` returns `"latest"` for such binaries. Users enabling FIPS mode purely via `GODEBUG` may believe they are using a validated module when they are not.

**Suggested improvement:** The documentation should explicitly state that running with `GODEBUG=fips140=on` on a binary not built with `GOFIPS140` uses the **latest** and **potentially unvalidated module version**. Suggested change:
>
> If set to `on`, FIPS 140-3 mode is enabled. If `GOFIPS140` was not set at build time, `latest` module will be used.
>
> If set to `only`, FIPS 140-3 mode is enabled as if set to `on`, and additionally cryptographic algorithms that are not FIPS 140-3 compliant will return an error or panic. Note that this is a best effort mode meant for testing, assessment, and debugging. It is not intended to be used in production, it is not required by the Security Policy, it introduces crashes and potentially unhandled errors by design, and it may have false positives or false negatives.
>
> Most programs should not set this option directly due to lack of control over the exact crypto module used, and should instead use GOFIPS140 at build time.

triage.title: proposal: net: IP.IsPrivate is widely misused as a security primitive — extend semantics and improve documentation
triage.body:
## Summary

`net.IP.IsPrivate` (and the matching method on `netip.Addr`) is repeatedly misused across the Go ecosystem as the basis for SSRF deny-lists, yielding a steady stream of high-severity CVEs. A Go networking maintainer has publicly stated that the method "was a mistake" because of this misuse, but the documentation contains no warning to that effect, and the method itself does not cover several address forms — most notably **IPv6 transition mechanisms that embed RFC 1918 / loopback IPv4 addresses** — that any reasonable interpretation of "private" should include.

This issue proposes:

1. **Primary:** Extend `IsPrivate` to return `true` for addresses that **represent connections to RFC 1918 / RFC 4193 destinations via well-defined address-family translation**, specifically: 6to4 (RFC 3056), Teredo (RFC 4380), NAT64 well-known prefix (RFC 6052 + RFC 8215), IPv4-mapped / IPv4-compatible IPv6 (RFC 4291), and ISATAP-style embedded IPv4 (RFC 5214) — in each case decoding the embedded IPv4 and applying the existing RFC 1918 check. This is a transitivity argument: if the address routes to a private IPv4 destination through a documented translation gateway, it is operationally private.

2. **Secondary (acknowledged contestable):** Consider adding RFC 6598 Carrier-Grade NAT (`100.64.0.0/10`) to `IsPrivate`'s scope. CGNAT space is widely used as private allocation by ISPs and mesh-VPN products (Tailscale, Netbird), but Python's stdlib explicitly chose *not* to include CGNAT in `is_private` on the basis that CGNAT is globally routable from the carrier's perspective. I'm noting this as a possible extension but would not block the rest of the proposal on it; the IPv6-transition extensions in item (1) are the more clearly correct ask.

3. **Fallback / minimum bar:** Add explicit security-misuse warnings to the doc comments of `IsPrivate`, `IsGlobalUnicast`, `IsLoopback`, `IsLinkLocalUnicast`, `IsMulticast`, and `IsUnspecified` — both in `net.IP` and `netip.Addr` — pointi

triage.title: x/crypto/argon2: Argon2 suggested parameters mismatch
triage.body:
The comments (rendered as documentation), suggest sets of parameters that do not correspond to the referenced RFC ([9106](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9106/#name-parameter-choice)).

While the first suggestions correctly suggest to take t=3 for Argon2i (lines 20-21) and t=1 for Argon2id (lines 30-31) and then maximize the memory (as per the RFC, section 7.3), then at lines 62 and 88 are suggested two sets of parameters (Argon2i with t=3, m=2^15 and Argon2id with t=1, m=2^16 respectively) that are not aligned with the suggestions in the RFC.
In fact, the first recommended option of the RFC is Argon2id with t=1, m=2^21 (section 4 and 7.4), while the second recommended option is Argon2id with t=3, m=2^16.
The parameter p is correctly set as p=4 as per suggestions of RFC, Section 4.

I would also suggest to include the other suggested parameters sets mentioned in the RFC (Section 4) especially because they mention explicit use cases which help to better understand how to correctly choose the parameters:

- Backend server authentication (targeting 0.5 seconds on a 2 GHz CPU using 4 cores): Argon2id with t=1, p=8, m=2^22 (4 GiB);
- Key derivation for hard-drive encryption (targeting 3 seconds on a 2 GHz CPU using 2 cores): Argon2id with t=1, p=4, m=3*2^21 (6 GiB);
- Frontend server authentication (targeting 0.5 seconds on a 2 GHz CPU using 2 cores): Argon2id with t=1, p=4, m=2^20 (1 GiB).

triage.title: proposal: spec: document that certain composite types have a fixed (but unspecified) size independent of composition
triage.body:
This is a proposal for a small addition to the language spec. Specifically we state:

> The sizes of slice, pointer, function, interface, map, and channel types are fixed, implementation-dependent constants specific to the kind of type (slice, pointer, etc.) but _independent of the specific composition of the type_.

For instance, this would state that an interface type is a fixed n bytes, known to the compiler, where n doesn't change irrespective of the interface composition, but n is not further specified. And similarly for all the other types mentioned above.

This would allow type-checking of cases that we currently do not permit such as:

```Go
type A *[unsafe.Sizeof(A{})]byte  // ERROR invalid recursive type: A refers to itself
```

Because the size of a pointer is fixed (even if unspecified), the expression `unsafe.Sizeof(A{})` does not depend on `A` and thus there is no cycle here. This is of course true already, but we don't state this in the spec and thus we don't depend on it for the purpose of detecting cycles.

Note that the spec already [says](https://tip.golang.org/ref/spec#Package_unsafe):

> A (variable of) type T has variable size if T is a [type parameter](https://tip.golang.org/ref/spec#Type_parameter_declarations), or if it is an array or struct type containing elements or fields of variable size. Otherwise the size is constant.

but this only says the size is constant for a specific such type; in fact it may be a different constant for different structs. In contrast, this proposal states (for the types mentioned in the proposal) that their sizes are always the same (but not furter specified) on a given platform. A program can determine the size via `unsafe.Sizeof`.

**Discussion**

- The benefit to "real" programs is largely marginal. Code such as the above example is esoteric at best and likely artificial. Some real-world examples would be nice to have.
- The impact on the language spec would be minimal: likely just an extra sentence or two in

triage.title: x/tour: minor confusion of array and slice length
triage.body:
The page about automatic slice ends at https://go.dev/tour/moretypes/10 reads (emphasis mine):

> The default is zero for the low bound and the **_length of the slice_** for the high bound.

This is a bit confusing because up to that point, slices have always been generated from arrays, not slices. My first thought was "oh, you mean the length of the _array_ for the high bound", which is indeed conformant to the example in the text. But in the code example on the right, slicing from a slice is introduced, so the full meaning is probably something along the lines of "length of the _underlying array or slice_".

As the result of slicing is also a slice, the term "length of the slice" could further be mistaken (in confusion) to mean the length of the resulting slice (however that might work), that's why I'd suggest adding the word "underlying".

triage.title: proposal: explicitly exclude error messages from the Go 1 compatibility promise
triage.body:
[The document that specifies the Go 1 compatibility promise](https://go.dev/doc/go1compat#expectations) ("go1compat" for short) lists a number of exclusions:

> - Security. A security issue in the specification or implementation may come to light whose resolution requires breaking compatibility. We reserve the right to address such security issues.
> - Unspecified behavior. The Go specification tries to be explicit about most properties of the language, but there are some aspects that are undefined. Programs that depend on such unspecified behavior may break in future releases.
> - [...]

However, there's no explicit exclusion for error messages. You perhaps don't perceive such omission as problematic. [In his GopherCon 2020 talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IKoSsJFdRtI&t=581s), @jba stated

> [...] we all understand that the text of error messages is for people and for people only. It is emphatically not part of the API like values and types are.

Arguably, most seasoned Gophers implicitly understand this: the wording of error messages falls outside the go1compat, it may change from one release to the next, and programs should not depend on the result of an error's `Error` method (e.g. via string matching).

However, this exclusion may not be obvious to all Gophers, esp. newcomers to the language; and some Gophers may be aware of it but fail to anticipate how disregarding it makes their programs brittle. [A casual search on GitHub](https://github.com/search?q=language%3AGo+%2Fstrings%5C.Contains%5C%28%5Cw%2B%5C.Error%5C%28%5C%29%2C%2F&type=code) indeed reveals that distressingly many Go programs do rely on string matching to extract data from error messages or distinguish one failure condition from another. Not only does this lack of clarity about error messages fail to discourage bad practices, it somewhat hinders the evolution of code covered by the go1compat. [A recent enough example](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.2:src/net/http/reque

triage.title: time: (docs) inaccurate description of Time.IsZero()
triage.body:
From [the docs](https://pkg.go.dev/time#Time):

> ..., the [Time.IsZero](https://pkg.go.dev/time#Time.IsZero) method gives a simple way of detecting a time that **has not been initialized** explicitly.

I believe this description of `Time.IsZero()` is inaccurate. Time initialized with `time.Time{}.In(nonUTC)` returns `.IsZero()` as true, eventhough it's not equal to uninitialized time.

I think we can update the description to something like:

> ..., the [Time.IsZero](https://pkg.go.dev/time#Time.IsZero) method gives a simple way of detecting a time that **equals to the zero time instant**.

### What did you do?

https://go.dev/play/p/qxQMCDIlrDD

```go
nonUTC := time.FixedZone("UTC-8", -8*60*60) // or any other non UTC location
t := time.Time{}.In(nonUTC)
fmt.Println(t) // 0000-12-31 16:00:00 -0800 UTC-8
fmt.Println(t.IsZero()) // true
fmt.Println(t == time.Time{}) // false
```

### Related issue

This was mentioned in https://github.com/golang/go/issues/57040#issuecomment-1335603244, but I don't think it's directly related since the issue focus more into the missing information when marshalling with json rather than the correctness of the documentation.

triage.title: regexp: repeat count limit is lower than documented
triage.body:
[regexp/syntax](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp/syntax) tells about a repeat count limit at 1000, but for some cases it is lower (250). Those cases should be documented.

### Go version

go version go1.26.1 darwin/arm64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
N/A
```

### What did you do?

On the [Go Playground](https://go.dev/play/p/nIKVTCl-CN1):
```go
var (
	ok1 = regexp.MustCompile(`(?:[a-z]{4}){0,250}`)
	ok2 = regexp.MustCompile(`(?:[a-z]{4}){0,250}(?:[a-z]{4})?`)
	// Doc of regexp in Go 1.26 says:
	// > Implementation restriction: The counting forms x{n,m}, x{n,}, and x{n} reject
	// > forms that create a minimum or maximum repetition count above 1000.
	// But this is rejected:
	fail = regexp.MustCompile(`(?:[a-z]{4}){0,251}`)
)
```

### What did you see happen?

```
panic: regexp: Compile(`(?:[a-z]{4}){0,251}`): error parsing regexp: invalid repeat count: `{0,251}`

goroutine 1 [running]:
regexp.MustCompile({0x4b13d6, 0x13})
	/usr/local/go-faketime/src/regexp/regexp.go:313 +0xb4
main.init()
	/tmp/sandbox1168500107/prog.go:12 +0x8d
```

### What did you expect to see?

The documentation of `regexp/syntax` ([Go 1.26.1](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp/syntax@go1.26.1), [latest](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp/syntax)) says about repetitions:
> Implementation restriction: The counting forms x{n,m}, x{n,}, and x{n} reject forms that create a minimum or maximum repetition count above 1000. Unlimited repetitions are not subject to this restriction. 

As the example shows, the restriction is lower for some cases, 250 here. Those cases must be better documented (and changes advertised in release notes).

triage.title: cmd/go: decide and document official recommendation for typical 'go' version in go.mod for open source libraries
triage.body:
This is somewhat related to the recent discussion in #77653, but I think this would be nice to do regardless of whatever the conclusion might be for #77653.

### Background

For open source libraries that intend to be used by the general ecosystem, there has been somewhat of an understanding that it is best for them to support at least the two officially supported versions of Go -- that is, the two newest major release versions of 1.N and 1.N-1, such as Go 1.26 and Go 1.25 currently.

Some open source libraries choose to support more than that, and some open source libraries might choose to support less than that, but the norm is often at least the 2 most recent versions if the intent is for an open source library to be widely used.

This choice became much more important due to the nice forward compatibility enhancements in #57001 ("proposal: extended forwards compatibility for Go").

During that conversation, one thing [I had suggested](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/57001#issuecomment-1387444294) was:

> One thing to think about might be something official or some semi-official statement from the Go project about expected norms for an open source project in terms of how quickly new Go semantics are adopted (that is, how quickly a project's go line is updated), especially for public modules consumed as libraries, tools that appear within go.mod files, and so on. That might help it not be too fast, as well as help reduce debate on various open source issue trackers about when to update.

I think Russ [seemed to agree](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/57001#issuecomment-1387453932) with that:

> A statement about expected norms in docs sounds good.

### Examples of on-going confusion

This is still a fairly common topic on open source projects (for example, as people open up drive-by PRs or debate what it should be in sometimes long and often confusing discussions on an issue).

triage.title: cmd/go: document GOROOT/bin/go PATH entry for `go run` and `go tool`
triage.body:
This is a continuation of issue #57050, to add missing documentation for a cmd/go behavior that's already implemented for a few more of its commands. ([CL 461683](https://go.dev/cl/461683) previously resolved this for `go test` and `go generate`.)

[CL 593255](https://go.dev/cl/593255) (in Go 1.24) changed `go run` to always place `GOROOT/bin` at the beginning of the `PATH` list for the subprocess, catching up and making it consistent with `go test` and `go generate`. However, the documentation for the command hasn't been updated. To permit users to comfortably rely on this behavior, it needs to be explicitly mentioned in the documentation for [`go run`](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/cmd/go/internal/run/run.go;l=26-61;drc=5f8fdb720c21873a8007b6c08aa9a5aee2125f76).

[CL 631836](https://go.dev/cl/631836) (in Go 1.24) similarly changed `go tool`, which as of [Go 1.24](https://go.dev/doc/modules/managing-dependencies#tools) can run commands tracked using tool directives in go.mod and not just those shipped with the Go distribution, to implement the same behavior of prepending `GOROOT/bin` at the beginning of `PATH`. Again, users can't rely on this until it's explicitly mentioned in the documentation for [`go tool`](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/cmd/go/internal/tool/tool.go;l=40-57;drc=5f8fdb720c21873a8007b6c08aa9a5aee2125f76).

CC @golang/command-line.

triage.title: net/http: Client preserves Request.Host across scheme relative redirects
triage.body:
When following a scheme-relative redirect, `http.Client` retains the original request's Host value rather than using the host from the redirect. This only applies when `Request.Host` is explicitly set to something other than `Request.URL`'s host. For example, when sending a request where `Request.URL` is `https://a.go.dev` and `Request.Host` is `b.go.dev`, a redirect to `//c.go.dev/` will cause the client to send a request to the address `c.go.dev` with a Host header of `b.go.dev` (instead of the correct `c.go.dev`).

This was reported to us as a potential security bug. We consider it to be an ordinary bug.

triage.title: os/exec: Cmd.Start on Windows can execute .bat/.cmd files from Cmd.Dir instead of Cmd.Path
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-generated summary. This issue was reported to us as a potential security bug. We are classifying this as a bug and security hardening measure, but not a vulnerability. (This was originally reported as #21675, which was declared working as intended. However, that predated #43724, which added the ErrDot security model.)

On Windows, when exec.Command resolves a bare command name (such as "tool" or "tool.bat") via LookPath to a .bat or .cmd file in PATH, setting Cmd.Dir causes Cmd.Start to execute a matching executable in Cmd.Dir instead of the resolved Cmd.Path.

Minimal reproduction:

```go
package main

import (
        "fmt"
        "os"
        "os/exec"
        "path/filepath"
)

func main() {
        base, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "repro")
        defer os.RemoveAll(base)
        safe := filepath.Join(base, "safe")
        work := filepath.Join(base, "work")
        os.MkdirAll(safe, 0755)
        os.MkdirAll(work, 0755)

        os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(safe, "tool.bat"), []byte("@echo SAFE\r\n"), 0755)
        os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(work, "tool.bat"), []byte("@echo WORK\r\n"), 0755)

        os.Setenv("PATH", safe+";"+os.Getenv("PATH"))

        cmd := exec.Command("tool") // resolves cmd.Path to safe\tool.bat
        cmd.Dir = work
        out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
        fmt.Printf("cmd.Path: %s\n", cmd.Path)
        fmt.Printf("output:   %q (err=%v)\n", out, err)
}
```

triage.title: mime, mime/multipart: ParseMediaType decodes RFC 2231 extended parameters as multipart boundaries
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-generated summary. The contents seem accurate to me. This was reported to us as a potential security bug. We are not classifying it as a security bug, but consider it a misbehavior which should be fixed as a hardening measure.

----

`mime.ParseMediaType` decodes RFC 2231 extended parameters (`param*=`) and continuations for all MIME parameters, overwriting any plain parameter of the same name (`param=`). When used with `Content-Type: multipart/...` headers in `net/http` and `mime/multipart`, this creates two issues:

1. **Parser differential on `boundary*` vs. `boundary`**: If a `Content-Type` header specifies `boundary*=utf-8''Y` (either alone or alongside `boundary=X`), `mime.ParseMediaType` returns `boundary="Y"`. While [RFC 6266 §4.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6266#section-4.3) specifies that `filename*` takes precedence over `filename` in `Content-Disposition` headers, intermediaries (proxies, WAFs) generally do not apply RFC 2231 decoding to the multipart `boundary` parameter in `Content-Type`. An intermediary inspecting `boundary=X` will parse a different set of multipart parts than a Go server using `boundary=Y`.
2. **Unvalidated characters in multipart boundaries**: RFC 2231 percent-decoding (`percentHexUnescape` in `src/mime/mediatype.go`) allows arbitrary percent-encoded bytes such as `%0D%0A` (CRLF) or other control characters that cannot appear in a plain token or quoted-string parameter. Neither `net/http` (`Request.MultipartReader` / `Request.ParseMultipartForm`) nor `mime/multipart.NewReader` validates that the boundary conforms to the [RFC 2046 §5.1.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2046#section-5.1.1) grammar (1–70 characters from the restricted `bchars` set, excluding control characters and CRLF).

triage.title: cmd/internal/obj/wasm: V128Store offset is always encoded as 0
triage.body:
### What happened

`AV128Store` is the only store opcode absent from `unaryDst` in `src/cmd/internal/obj/wasm/wasmobj.go`. Every other store is listed: `AI32Store`, `AI64Store`, `AF32Store`, `AF64Store`, `AI32Store8`, `AI32Store16`, `AI64Store8`, `AI64Store16`, `AI64Store32`.

`appendp` routes a single argument based on that membership:

```go
case 1:
	if unaryDst[as] {
		p.From = obj.Addr{}
		p.To = args[0]
	} else {
		p.From = args[0]
		p.To = obj.Addr{}
	}
```

So `appendp(p, AV128Store, constAddr(offset))` stores the offset in `p.From` and zeroes `p.To`. But `assemble` reads the offset for that whole group from `p.To`:

```go
case AI32Store, AI64Store, AF32Store, AF64Store, AI32Store8, AI32Store16, AI64Store8, AI64Store16, AI64Store32, AV128Store:
	if p.To.Offset < 0 {
		panic("negative offset")
	}
	if p.To.Offset > math.MaxUint32 {
		ctxt.Diag("bad offset in %v", p)
	}
	writeUleb128(w, align(p.As))
	writeUleb128(w, uint64(p.To.Offset))
```

The result is that the memory offset encoded for every `v128.store` is 0, whatever offset the caller passed.

### Where it is reachable

Both wrapper generators use the one-argument form:

  - `wasmobj.go:880`, the `//go:wasmimport` wrapper
  - `wasmobj.go:946`, the `//go:wasmexport` wrapper

In both, the `AF64Store` line immediately above is correct, because `AF64Store` is in `unaryDst`.

`obj.WasmV128` is produced by `ssagen/abi.go:435` and `:480` when `t.IsSIMD()`, so this is reached by a `//go:wasmimport` or `//go:wasmexport` function with a SIMD-typed field. That requires `GOEXPERIMENT=SIMD`, so no default build is affected today, which is presumably why it has gone unnoticed.

Verified on master at dfc6f7db9b.

Adding `AV128Store` to `unaryDst` makes it consistent with every other store and routes the offset to `p.To`, which is where `assemble` reads it.

triage.title: runtime: each exited thread leaks a semaphore on AIX
triage.body:
### Go version

go version go1.27.2 aix/ppc64 (also tip, go1.28-devel_dfc6f7db9b)

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOARCH='ppc64'
GOOS='aix'
CGO_ENABLED='1'
CC='gcc'
```

### What did you do?

Relates to #82244.

Ran a program that repeatedly starts a goroutine which locks its thread, parks once, and returns while still locked, so the runtime exits the thread.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	_ "runtime/cgo"
)

func main() {
	for i := 1; i <= 40000; i++ {
		done := make(chan bool)
		go func() {
			runtime.LockOSThread()
			runtime.Gosched() // park the locked thread once
			close(done)
		}() // returns while locked, so the runtime exits the thread
		<-done
		if i%5000 == 0 {
			fmt.Println(i)
		}
	}
	fmt.Println("ok")
}
```

This imports `runtime/cgo` only because without cgo, exited threads do not actually exit on AIX (#82244), so the program would stall on that bug first. If applied, the program fails the same way without the `runtime/cgo` import and with `CGO_ENABLED=0`.

### What did you see happen?

Output in about 3 seconds:

```
5000
10000
15000
20000

uuid: speed up UUID.Compare by implementing it with bytes.Compare
triage.body:
## Summary

[uuid.UUID#Compare](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/dfc6f7db9bd75868ffb5cbc9501a2f4899122d2f/src/uuid/uuid.go#L168-L184) currently compares one byte at a time using `cmp.Compare`.
As a result, the number of comparisons grows with the length of the matching prefix, and comparing two equal UUIDs requires 16 comparisons.

```go
func (u UUID) Compare(v UUID) int {
    for i := range u {
        if c := cmp.Compare(u[i], v[i]); c != 0 {
            return c
        }
    }
    return 0
}
```

I propose replacing it with `bytes.Compare`.

```go
func (u UUID) Compare(v UUID) int {
    return bytes.Compare(u[:], v[:])
}
```

On arm64, `bytes.Compare` is implemented in assembly in [internal/bytealg/compare_arm64.s](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/dfc6f7db9bd75868ffb5cbc9501a2f4899122d2f/src/internal/bytealg/compare_arm64.s).
For a 16-byte input, it loads the 16 bytes into two 8-byte registers with a single `LDP` instruction and finishes the comparison with **only two** 64-bit `CMP` instructions.
The position of the differing byte does not matter.

## Benchmarks

- go1.27.2 / darwin/arm64 / Apple M4 Max, `-count 10`, benchstat
- `DiffN` compares two UUIDs that differ only at byte N (0-indexed).

triage.title: security: fix CVE-2026-97032
triage.body:
net/http: HTTP/2 server crash due to HPACK encoder race

HTTP/2 servers could end up crashing due to inadvertently
modifying its HPACK encoder concurrently. This happens because the
server modifies the HPACK encoder from two goroutines without
synchronization: one uses the encoder to encode a HEADERS frame as part
of a response sent to a client and the other modifies the encoder's
table size when handling a SETTINGS frame containing
SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE that a client sends. A malicious client can
repeatedly send a request while changing the header table size to crash
the server.

Fix this issue by not applying SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE immediately.
Instead, buffer any SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE received, and only apply
the new value prior to the next time the server writes a frame.

Thanks to RyotaK (https://ryotak.net) of GMO Flatt Security Inc. for reporting this issue.

This is CVE-2026-97032 and Go issue https://go.dev/issue/81867.

---

This was a [PRIVATE track](https://go.dev/doc/security/policy#private) issue originally tracked in http://b/539475988.

Found this while working on https://github.com/mauri870/loopvec.

Compiled and disassembled a loop that calls `Float32s.Neg`:

```go
package main

import "simd"

func neg(dst, a []float32) {
	for i := 0; i < len(dst); {
		v, n := simd.LoadFloat32sPart(a[i:])

	}

	a := make([]float32, 100)
	d := make([]float32, 100)
	neg(d, a)
}
```

```
GOEXPERIMENT=simd go build -o neg .
go tool objdump -s 'main\.neg@simd512$' neg
```

`neg` is a dispatcher that picks `neg@simd128`, `neg@simd256` or `neg@simd512`
on every call; the loop body lives in the width-specific clone.


### What did you see happen?

`Neg` lowers to an XOR with a sign-bit vector, but the instructions that
build that vector are emitted at the use site, inside the loop body, instead
of once before the loop. On `go1.27.1` the relevant part of `neg@simd512`

4a3947  VMOVDQU64 Z1, 0(R9)          ; full-width store
4a394d  JMP 0x4a3898                 ; back edge, before the constant rebuild

49d05c  MOVL $-0x80000000, DX        ; constant rebuilt every iteration
49d061  VMOVD DX, X1
49d065  VPBROADCASTD X1, Z1
49d071  VPXORD Z1, Z0, Z0
49d07e  VMOVDQU64 Z0, 0(R9)

	"fmt"
	"simd"

	for i := 0; i < len(pad); {

function fails to compile at all, seems to be a type-checking error,
not an internal compiler error.

triage.title: net/http: double flow control refund on HTTP/2 server streams
triage.body:
The HTTP/2 server could refund connection-level flow control twice for the same data:
Once when a client resets a stream (refunding data for any sent-but-unread portion
of the stream), and again when a request handler reads the buffered data.
A malicious client could exploit this to bypass the configured connection-level
flow control limit (MaxReceiveBufferPerConnection). Total buffered data is still
limited by the concurrent stream limit and stream-level flow control.

The HTTP/2 server now waits to refund connection-level flow control for reset
streams until after the request handler is complete.

Thanks to Ali Sherif (https://www.linkedin.com/in/ali-sherif-13812b276/) for reporting this issue.

This is CVE-2026-78663 and Go issue https://go.dev/issue/81743.

---

This was a [PRIVATE track](https://go.dev/doc/security/policy#private) issue originally tracked in http://b/549709976.

triage.title: net/http: excessive CPU consumption from repeated initial window changes
triage.body:
A malicious HTTP/2 peer could cause excessive CPU consumption in the
client or server by opening a large number of streams and then sending
many small SETTINGS frames containing SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE values.

The HTTP/2 client and server now efficiently handle changes to the
initial window size (O(1) rather than O(number of streams)).

Thanks to Jakub Ciolek (https://ciolek.dev) for reporting this issue.

This is CVE-2026-78669 and Go issue https://go.dev/issue/81742.

As reported in #81385, the tools/go/ssa package has a lot of very subtle quirks when it comes to generic methods. There now exists a lot of one off fixes when lowering functions and methods into SSA form, to handle receivers/generic type params/method exprs/etc. These fixes cause the code to become harder to understand and more brittle, as different parts of the package have to know and expect for the one off fixes without them being explicit in the type system.

We would ideally have minimal SSA specific type transformations during the lowering process, so that the SSA code is more resilient to changes upstream in the language.
