triage.title: net/http/cgi: RequestFromMap can set r.URL.Host to a different value than r.Host
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-generated summary. This issue was reported to us as a potential security issue. We do not consider this to be a security but, because it requires the invoking HTTP server to pass an invalid HTTP_HOST value to the CGI program, which no reasonable server will. Probably still worth fixing as general hardening.

`cgi.RequestFromMap` (also used by `net/http/fcgi`) constructs the request URL by concatenating `HTTP_HOST` (`r.Host`) and `REQUEST_URI` (`uriStr` / `SCRIPT_NAME`) and passing the combined string `"http://" + r.Host + uriStr` to `url.Parse`:

```go
r.Host = params["HTTP_HOST"]
rawurl := r.Host + uriStr
rawurl = "http://" + rawurl
url, err := url.Parse(rawurl)
r.URL = url
```

If HTTP_HOST contains an @ character (e.g., HTTP_HOST="example.com@other.com", REQUEST_URI="/path") or if REQUEST_URI does not start with / and begins with @ (e.g., HTTP_HOST="example.com", REQUEST_URI="@other.com/path"), url.Parse interprets the prefix before @ as the URL userinfo component. This results in r.URL.Host ("other.com") diverging from r.Host.

RequestFromMap should validate r.Host / uriStr or parse the URI path separately from r.Host so that r.URL.Host cannot diverge from r.Host.

triage.title: net/http/cgi: PathLocationHandler local redirects starting with "//" overwrite Request.Host
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-written summary. This issue was reported to us as a potential security issue. We feel that this is a bug, but not one we are classifying as a vulnerability.

In `net/http/cgi`, when `Handler.PathLocationHandler` is set and a CGI script responds with a `Location` header starting with `"/"`, `Handler` treats it as a local redirect (RFC 3875 §6.2.2) and dispatches it internally via `handleInternalRedirect`:

```go
url, err := req.URL.Parse(urlstr)
if err != nil {
    ...
}
newReq := &http.Request{
    Method:   "GET",
    URL:      url,
    Proto:    "HTTP/1.1",
    ProtoMajor: 1,
    ProtoMinor: 1,
    Header:   make(http.Header),
    Host:     url.Host,
    RemoteAddr: req.RemoteAddr,
    TLS:      req.TLS,
}
```

If the Location header begins with "//" (e.g., Location: //example.internal/path), `strings.HasPrefix(location, "/")` classifies it as a local path redirect, but `req.URL.Parse` parses "//example.internal/path" as a network-path reference (url.Host = "example.internal", url.Path = "/path") and sets `newReq.Host = url.Host`, replacing the original `req.Host` rather than preserving it and treating location strictly as a local path.

triage.title: net/url: URL.String turns Path into Host when Host is empty, User is non-nil, and Path has no leading slash
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-written summary. The summary seems accurate to me. This was reported to us as a potential security issue. We feel that this is a bug, but we are classifying this as security hardening rather than a vulnerability.

In `net/url`, `(*URL).String` writes the `//userinfo@` prefix whenever `u.User != nil`, even if `u.Host == ""`, and only prepends
a leading `/` to `u.Path` when `u.Host != ""` and `u.Path` does not already begin with `/`.

As a result, when `u.Host == ""`, `u.User != nil`, and `u.Path` does not start with `/`, `u.String()` concatenates `//userinfo@`
directly with `u.Path`, causing the first segment of `u.Path` to be parsed as `Host` if the string is reparsed:

```go
u, _ := url.Parse("example.com/path") // Scheme="", Host="", Path="example.com/path"
u.Scheme = "https"
u.User = url.User("user")

s := u.String() // "https://user@example.com/path"
u2, _ := url.Parse(s)
fmt.Println(u2.Host) // "example.com"
```

(Related to #78328.)

triage.title: x/image/webp: DecodeConfig returns YCbCr/NYCbCrA ColorModel for VP8X+VP8L images while Decode   returns NRGBA
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-written summary; I have not verified its validity, but it seems plausible. This issue was reported to us as a potential security bug. While it's clearly a bug in `webp.DecodeConfig`, we do not believe it has interesting security implications.

In `golang.org/x/image/webp`, `decode` (`webp/decode.go`, `case fccVP8X:`) returns early when `configOnly` is true (`DecodeConfig`), choosing `image.Config.ColorModel` (`color.NYCbCrAModel` or `color.YCbCrModel`) solely from the `VP8X` header's alpha flag without inspecting the subsequent image data chunk.

When `configOnly` is false (`Decode`), execution continues to the next chunk. If the image data chunk is `VP8L` (lossless WebP inside an extended `VP8X` container, such as `testdata/gopher-doc.with-alpha.lossless.webp`), `vp8l.Decode` returns an `*image.NRGBA` whose  `ColorModel()` is `color.NRGBAModel`:

```go
cfg, _ := webp.DecodeConfig(bytes.NewReader(gopherDocWithAlphaLosslessBytes))
fmt.Println(cfg.ColorModel) // color.NYCbCrAModel

img, _ := webp.Decode(bytes.NewReader(gopherDocWithAlphaLosslessBytes))
fmt.Println(img.ColorModel()) // color.NRGBAModel (*image.NRGBA)
```

As a result, DecodeConfig and Decode disagree on the ColorModel of VP8X+VP8L WebP files (and when the VP8X alpha bit is cleared on a VP8X+VP8L file, DecodeConfig reports color.YCbCrModel while Decode still returns color.NRGBAModel).

triage.title: x/image/vp8l: buildSimple assigns non-canonical Huffman codewords when symbols[0] >= symbols[1]
x/image/vp8: int32 overflow in inverseDCT4 produces incorrect decoded pixels
triage.body:
The following is an LLM-written summary; I have not verified its validity, but it seems plausible. This issue was reported to us as a potential security bug. Image misparsing is actually the canonical example of "not every bug is a security bug" in our [security decisions](https://go.dev/doc/security/decisions#principles).

In `golang.org/x/image/vp8`, `inverseDCT4` (`vp8/idct.go`) multiplies dequantized `int16` coefficients (`z.coeff`) by `c1 = 85627` using `int32` arithmetic:

```go
c := (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+4])*c1)>>16 + (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+12])*c2)>>16
d := (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+4])*c2)>>16 - (int32(z.coeff[coeffBase+12])*c1)>>16
```

When a dequantized coefficient's magnitude exceeds 25079 (math.MaxInt32 / 85627)—for example, an AC token value v = 89 with quant = 284 (base_q = 127) yielding 25276—the product int32(coeff) * c1 overflows int32 and wraps around, flipping the sign of the intermediate term and producing corrupted output pixels that diverge from libwebp (dwebp).

libwebp (TransformOne_C in src/dsp/dec.c) avoids this overflow by decomposing the multiplication as ((a * 20091) >> 16) + a (where 20091 + 65536 = 85627), or the multiplication in inverseDCT4 can be performed in int64.

triage.title: runtime: speed up GC phase transitions
triage.body:
```
go version go1.28-devel_d27b23f671 Wed Sep 16 18:07:03 2026 -0700 darwin/arm64
```

I've been looking at how the GC coordinates across all Ps, for the GC's ragged barriers and STWs. (Most of my data is from the runtime package's "BenchmarkAllocation"; with GOGC=100 there are hundreds or thousands of GCs per second, so most of what it's benchmarking is the effect of STW delays on application throughput.)

For the stop-the-world events, I see that most of the wall-clock cost is from bringing the world to a stop, rather than slow bookkeeping in the STW's critical section.

I also see that `forEachP`, especially as used during GC phase transitions, causes pileups on `sched.lock` by 1/ holding it for a long time, while 2/ inducing demand for it on other Ms.

We should reduce the wall-clock time required for ragged barriers and to stop-the-world.

---

Some STWs see delay because after some Ps have begun to transition to "idle", a "running" P can still _pick up and start running_ a G. The delay between the announcement of the STW and the start of that goroutine's run can be in the neighborhood of 50µs.

The path for a spinning M to steal a P's `runnext` slot includes a delay. The `runnext` slot enables cheap context switches between goroutines (which share a time slice) within a P, and unnecessary migration would defeat that optimization. Platforms with "fast" timers implement the delay as `usleep(3)`. On Linux, the kernel pads that with some timer slack. In my testing, calls to `usleep(3)` on linux/amd64 usually take 50–60µs.

The spinning M verifies that the target P is running before committing to that sleep. The problem arises when a STW begins _during_ the sleep. The spinning M wakes up, easily steals the `runnext` G (the victim P is now idle, honoring the STW request), and starts running it.

triage.title: net/http: be stricter about framing-related headers
triage.body:
This is a follow up to #81115.

#81115 describes an issue where:
1. A server sends multiple conflicting `Content-Length` headers.
2. A reverse proxy, using our HTTP/2 transport implementation, accepts the headers and passes them along to the client (normally, this is okay to do since HTTP/2 framing does not rely on `Content-Length` headers).
3. An HTTP/1 client, which improperly accepts multiple `Content-Length` headers (our HTTP/1 transport does not), is now vulnerable to response smuggling.

After #81115, our HTTP/2 transport will no longer forward multiple `Content-Length` headers, just in case we are forwarding to an HTTP/1 implementation that might be vulnerable to response smuggling.

However, it might be beneficial for us to be stricter about framing-related headers in general:
1. Our server should not send an HTTP/1 response containing multiple `Content-Length` headers.
2. Consider similar scenarios with non-canonical (e.g., `content-length` rather than `Content-Length`).
3. Consider similar scenarios with `Transfer-Encoding`.

A dedicated attacker can always directly send invalid framing-related headers to the wire regardless of our implementation. But, this can prevent cases where someone using our server accidentally sends bad headers.

triage.title: simd/archsimd: clean up "emulated" doc comments
triage.body:
Today, we have various operations in `archsimd` marked "Emulated" as such:

```go
// GreaterEqual returns a mask whose elements indicate whether x >= y.
//
// Emulated, CPU Feature: AVX
func (x Int8x16) GreaterEqual(y Int8x16) Mask8x16
```

There are several things that could be better about this:
1. It doesn't follow the same convention as other implementation notes, which (almost) all start with "Keyword:", like "Asm:", "CPU Feature:", or a few others. I'm in the process of building the tooling to combine semantics-level doc comments from spec with implementation-level doc comments like this and the inconsistency makes this messy.
2. It's not very informative. We don't do an emulation if it would be expensive, but you might care whether it's emulated with 2 instructions or 10.
3. Sometimes we mark operations as emulated that are literally a single operation. For example, x.Less(y) is "emulated" as y.Greater(x). That means we don't have an "Asm:" block, but is this really an "emulation"?

I spent a while exploring solutions, but reached my time-box. A few options:

1. Assume that, if a user cares, they'll just look at the body to see how it's emulated. It would be nice to fit the "Keyword:" convention, but it's really just a flag.
2. List the methods it's defined in terms of, like "Emulated: Xor, Greater", excluding no-op conversions. This stays pretty high-level, which is nice, and gives a direct sense of the emulation complexity/cost. But it's surprisingly annoying to hand write: It can drift easily from the implementation if we're not careful; a bunch of these emulations are generated from complex, branchy-templates, which means doc comment needs the same template branches; and emulations are often written atop other emulations and ideally this would be the transitive closure, but that's even messier to maintain by hand. It's possible we could fully automate generating these comments with a little syntactic analysis.
3. List the assembly operations it's defined

triage.title: x/net/idna: Bidi rule evaluated before UTS 46 mapping
triage.body:
```go
a, err := idna.Lookup.ToASCII("a\u2135b")
fmt.Println(a, err)
fmt.Println(idna.Lookup.ToASCII(a))
```

Produces:

```
xn--ab-vld <nil>
xn--ab-vld idna: invalid label "xn--ab-vld"
```

"a\u2135b" and "xn--ab-vld" are the same domain label. This label violates the Bidi rule, but idna.Lookup.ToASCII accepts the Unicode form because it applies the Bidi rule before mapping U+2135 to U+05D0.

This was reported to us as a potential security vulnerability. We do not consider this to be a security bug, but it is a bug.

Thanks to Naseeb Dangi and Xiang Li from AOSP Lab @ Nankai University for reporting the issue.

triage.title: crypto/x509: reject unsupported bounds in critical name constraints
triage.body:
The name constraints parser ignores the contents of each GeneralSubtree after its base name, including `minimum` and `maximum` fields, and treats the critical extension as handled. As a result, verification can accept a chain with unsupported subtree bounds instead of processing those bounds or rejecting the certificate as required by RFC 5280.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

In `src/crypto/x509/parser.go`, `parseNameConstraintsExtension` reads a GeneralSubtree SEQUENCE and its first element but does not consume or check the remaining `seq`. `processExtensions` then considers the extension handled, and chain constraint checks operate only on the parsed base names.

A reproducer uses an Ed25519 root, intermediate, and leaf, with this critical nameConstraints extension (OID `2.5.29.30`) on the intermediate:

```go
// permittedSubtrees: dNSName "example.com", maximum [1] 0
badNC := []byte{0x30, 0x14, 0xa0, 0x12, 0x30, 0x10, 0x82, 0x0b,
    'e', 'x', 'a', 'm', 'p', 'l', 'e', '.', 'c', 'o', 'm', 0x81, 0x01, 0x00}
```

Give the leaf the DNS SAN `www.example.com`, trust the root, supply the intermediate, and call `leaf.Verify` with that DNS name and a time within all certificates' validity intervals. `UnhandledCriticalExtensions` is empty and verification returns nil, despite the unsupported maximum bound.

RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10 requires minimum zero and maximum absent within the profile. For a critical extension with other bounds on a name form used later in the path, an implementation must process the bounds or reject the certificate.

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: crypto/rsa: VerifyPSS accepts salts longer than the hash in FIPS-only mode
triage.body:
In FIPS 140-only mode, `VerifyPSS` rejects an explicitly requested salt length greater than the hash size, but accepts an otherwise valid signature with such a salt when using `PSSSaltLengthAuto`, including when `opts` is nil. The auto-detection path records a non-approved operation without returning an error.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

The `VerifyPSS` wrapper in `src/crypto/rsa/fips.go` checks `saltLength > h.Size()` before dispatching to the internal verifier. `PSSSaltLengthAuto` does not exceed that bound, so the wrapper delegates without constraining the actual salt length.

In `src/crypto/internal/fips140/rsa/pkcs1v22.go`, `emsaPSSVerify` detects the actual salt length and calls `fips140.RecordNonApproved()` when `sLen > hLen`, but verification can subsequently return nil. This conflicts with the FIPS-only requirement to prevent operations that make the module's service indicator false.

A regression test should generate an otherwise valid RSA-PSS signature outside FIPS-only mode with salt length `hash.Size()+1`, then verify it with `GODEBUG=fips140=only` and nil options or explicit `PSSSaltLengthAuto`. This concerns FIPS-only policy enforcement, not signature forgery.

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: crypto/tls: repeated ech_outer_extensions placeholders bypass reference ordering checks
triage.body:
`decodeInnerClientHello` processes multiple `ech_outer_extensions` placeholders without rejecting the duplicate placeholder. Each placeholder resets the outer-extension scan, allowing reconstruction to copy referenced extensions in a different relative order from ClientHelloOuter. The final ClientHello parser no longer sees the placeholders and cannot detect the invalid encoding.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

Place `supported_versions` (`0x002b`) before `key_share` (`0x0033`) in ClientHelloOuter. The encoded inner hello contains the inner ECH marker and two placeholders, with bodies `02 00 33` and `02 00 2b`. Each body is a well-formed one-entry vector, but together they copy `key_share` before `supported_versions`. RFC 9849 §5.1 requires the references to preserve their outer relative order.

In `src/crypto/tls/ech.go`, the scan cursor `i` is local to each placeholder, so the second scan starts from the beginning. Reconstruction removes both placeholders and produces distinct final extension IDs, avoiding the downstream duplicate-extension check.

Both initial and post-HelloRetryRequest ECH decoding use this path. An end-to-end regression test would need valid HPKE encryption and otherwise valid ClientHello fields; the two well-formed vectors above isolate the ordering issue from the separate trailing-data parsing bug.

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: crypto/tls: RSA key exchange accepts ciphertexts shorter than the modulus
triage.body:
`rsaKeyAgreement.processClientKeyExchange` checks the encrypted premaster-secret vector length against the message body, but not against the RSA modulus size. With a decrypter that accepts omitted leading zero bytes, a noncanonical ciphertext can return the original premaster secret and allow the handshake to complete.

Enforce the modulus-sized ciphertext encoding while preserving the RSA key-exchange countermeasures for invalid ciphertexts.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

To exercise the path with a normal `*rsa.PrivateKey`, or another decrypter with the same short-ciphertext behavior:

1. Encrypt a known 48-byte premaster secret until the modulus-sized ciphertext begins with `00`.
2. Remove that byte and encode the remaining `k-1` bytes with a matching two-byte TLS vector length, where `k` is the modulus size.
3. Use the known premaster secret to compute Finished.

The framing check in `src/crypto/tls/key_agreement.go` accepts this vector. Removing a leading zero preserves the RSA integer, so decryption with `rsa.PKCS1v15DecryptOptions{SessionKeyLen: 48}` can return the chosen secret rather than the random fallback.

This case requires an enabled RSA key-exchange cipher suite; it does not recover another connection’s secret or the server’s private key.

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: crypto/tls: decodeInnerClientHello discards trailing ech_outer_extensions data
triage.body:
`decodeInnerClientHello` accepts trailing bytes after the length-prefixed vector in `ech_outer_extensions`. It passes `extData` as both receiver and output to `ReadUint8LengthPrefixed`, replacing the parent string with the child vector before checking whether the parent was fully consumed.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

For extension data `02 00 2b ff`, the two-byte vector references `supported_versions` (`0x002b`), and `ff` is outside it. With a valid TLS 1.3 `supported_versions` extension in ClientHelloOuter and the inner ECH marker `01`, reconstruction copies the referenced extension and drops `ff`. The suffix is not interpreted as another extension identifier. RFC 9849 §5.1 permits only the `OuterExtensions` vector in this extension body.

The aliasing occurs in `src/crypto/tls/ech.go`. `cryptobyte.String.readLengthPrefixed` assigns the child to the output after consuming it, so aliasing loses the unconsumed suffix. Both `processECHClientHello` and the post-HelloRetryRequest server path reach this decoder; an end-to-end test of either path would require a valid HPKE payload and otherwise valid ClientHello fields.

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: crypto/tls: final ServerHello can accept ECH after HelloRetryRequest rejected it
triage.body:
The TLS 1.3 client can accept ECH in the final ServerHello after a HelloRetryRequest did not confirm ECH. In that case it switches to the saved inner transcript even though the HRR path did not construct or transcript a second ClientHelloInner.

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

A regression scenario requires a client configured with `EncryptedClientHelloConfigList` and a server that can decrypt ECH and authenticate for the inner name:

1. Send a cookie-only HRR without an ECH confirmation, or with an incorrect eight-byte confirmation.
2. Receive the second outer ClientHello. Since `isInnerHello` is false, the client has not added a second inner ClientHello to `innerTranscript`.
3. Select a key share offered in the first inner ClientHello and compute the final ServerHello confirmation over `message_hash(ClientHelloInner1) || HRR || ServerHelloWithZeroedConfirmation`.

In `src/crypto/tls/handshake_client_tls13.go`, the final confirmation check runs whenever `hs.echContext != nil`, regardless of HRR rejection. A match sets `c.echAccepted` and selects the incomplete inner transcript for the key schedule, CertificateVerify, and Finished. A server with the required keys can construct the remaining handshake messages using that transcript; this does not enable impersonation by a peer lacking the ECH key or authentication for the inner name.

RFC 9849 §§6.1.4, 6.1.5, and 7.2.1 require an accepted HRR flow to include the second inner ClientHello.

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: math/rand/v2: ChaCha8.UnmarshalBinary panics on an overlong read buffer
triage.body:
`(*ChaCha8).UnmarshalBinary` accepts a length-prefixed `readbuf:` field longer than its eight-byte buffer, then panics while slicing the buffer instead of returning an error. It also updates the buffered bytes before validating the remaining state, so a failed unmarshal can change subsequent `Read` output.

```go
c := rand.NewChaCha8([32]byte{}) // rand is math/rand/v2
_ = c.UnmarshalBinary([]byte("readbuf:\x09123456789")) // slice bounds panic
```

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

In `src/math/rand/v2/chacha8.go`, `UnmarshalBinary` executes `c.readLen = copy(c.readBuf[len(c.readBuf)-len(buf):], buf)` before calling `chacha8rand.Unmarshal`. The length-prefix helper accepts lengths from 0 through 255 if enough bytes follow. A nine-byte buffer makes the slice start at −1, before the core state is checked.

A shorter buffer avoids the panic but is committed even if the remaining state is invalid. On a fresh generator, the following rejected encoding injects `POC` into the next read:

```go
err := c.UnmarshalBinary([]byte("readbuf:\x03POCnot-a-valid-chacha8-state"))
var out [3]byte; _, _ = c.Read(out[:]) // err != nil; string(out[:]) == "POC"
```

</details>

This issue was found by [zkao](https://zkao.io) and was triaged by @FiloSottile as a valid bug but not a vulnerability. /cc @golang/security

triage.title: net/http/internal/http2: clean up x/net crufts
triage.body:
Our HTTP/2 implementation used to live in x/net, and there were two ways of using it:
1. Indirectly via `net/http`.
2. Directly via `x/net`.

As such, the code is littered with various logic and documentations that account for both modes of usage (e.g., was a connection dialed in `net/http` and then handed to HTTP/2? Or, did HTTP/2 dial it on its own?).

Now that HTTP/2 lives in `net/http/internal/http2` (#67810), many parts of the package that deal with direct usage from `x/net` are essentially dead / stale. Furthermore, various copied / similar implementations between `net/http` and HTTP/2 can now be consolidated.

This is an overall tracking bug for cleaning up all such clutters.

triage.title: crypto/tls: anyValidVerifiedChain doesn't consider cross-signatures
triage.body:
anyValidVerifiedChain is intended to check if a chain is rooted in a root that is still trusted. We do this by calling x509.Certificate.Verify on the root, which should short circuit in the internal map lookup.

If the root has been removed, but was cross-signed, a new chain could be built from the root to the cross-signature, with perhaps more restrictive policies, such as name constraints. Because of this, presence of such a chain from the original root to the new root doesn't imply the whole chain is still trusted.

We should probably either (a) only accept Verify results that provide a single certificate chain or (b) if we get a chain longer than one certificate, re-run Verify with the original chain _and_ the new certificates beyond the original root. (b) seems significantly more complicated, we should probably just go with (a).

Due to the limited impact of this issue, we are treating this as a PUBLIC track issue per the Go Security Policy (https://go.dev/security/policy).

This is CVE-2026-78666.

Thanks to Jakub Ciolek for originally reporting this.

triage.title: crypto/x509: uri constraints allow subdomain matching
triage.body:
Similar to #81280.

uniformResourceIdentifier constraints have weird semantics. We treat them as equivalent to dNSName constraints, but they are not exactly the same. In particular, they way we handle the leading period form of the constraint is not correct (we match subtrees when we should require exact matches).

Given the extreme rarity of name constraints, we are treating this as a PUBLIC track security issue, per the Go Security Policy (https://go.dev/security/policy).

This is CVE-2026-78665.

Thanks to Ali Sherif for originally reporting this.

triage.title: crypto/x509: email constraints allow subdomain matching
triage.body:
Confusing RFC 5280 constraint behavior strikes again.

rfc822Name constraints have weird URI adjacent semantics. Basically, the constraint "example.com" matches all inboxes for example.com (but not sub.example.com), whereas the constraint ".example.com" matches all inboxes for all subdomains of example.com (but not example.com!)

Currently, we treat the domain portion the same way we treat dNSName constraints, which is wrong.

Given the extreme rarity of name constraints, we are treating this as a PUBLIC track security issue, per the Go Security Policy (https://go.dev/security/policy).

This is CVE-2026-78664.

Thanks to Jack Lloyd for initially reporting this.

triage.title: debug/dwarf: LineReader panics with negative index on DW_LNS_set_file with file number ≥ 2⁶³
triage.body:
# debug/dwarf: LineReader panics on negative file index from DW_LNS_set_file

## Summary

`dwarf.LineReader` panics with a negative index when a line program executes
`DW_LNS_set_file` with a file number ≥ 2⁶³:

```
panic: runtime error: index out of range [-9223372036854775808]

goroutine 1 [running]:
debug/dwarf.(*LineReader).updateFile(...)
	src/debug/dwarf/line.go:469
debug/dwarf.(*LineReader).step(...)
	src/debug/dwarf/line.go:595
debug/dwarf.(*LineReader).Next(...)
	src/debug/dwarf/line.go:492
```

Verified on go1.23.3 and go1.27.0; master `line.go` has the same unguarded code.
Minimal self-contained repro (~50 bytes of handcrafted DWARF) available; also found
independently by mutating a real Go ELF (8-byte mutation), so trivially reachable by
fuzzing malware/attacker-supplied binaries.

## Root cause

`step()`'s `opSetFile` case reads a ULEB128 into an `int`
(`r.fileIndex = int(r.buf.uint())`, line ~594). Values ≥ 2⁶³ become negative.
`updateFile()` guards only the upper bound:

```go
if r.fileIndex < len(r.fileEntries) {   // line ~468 — no r.fileIndex >= 0 check
    r.file = &r.fileEntries[r.fileIndex]
}
```

A negative `fileIndex` passes the upper-bound check and indexes out of range.

## Impact

Tools feeding untrusted binaries to `debug/dwarf` (symbolizers, malware analysis
pipelines, delve-style debuggers reading core dumps) are killed by one malformed
`.debug_line` section. This class (panics on malformed binaries in debug/*) is
routinely accepted and fixed — #52354, #53329, #75130, #75516 — none of which cover
this site (different file, different failure).

## Suggested fix

Bounds-check both sides in `updateFile` (or validate the ULEB fits int and reject
negative at `step()`):

```go
if r.fileIndex >= 0 && r.fileIndex < len(r.fileEntries) {
```

Happy to send the patch — the minimal DWARF repro and the fuzzer-found variant are
both ready.

triage.title: archive/tar: mergePAX silently truncates UID/GID to 0 on integer overflow
triage.body:
### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?
go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64 (and master)

### What operating system and processor architecture are you using (`go env`)?
32-bit architectures (`GOARCH=386`, `GOARCH=arm`, `GOARCH=wasm`)

### What did you do?
Read a TAR archive containing a PAX header with `uid="4294967296"` (1 << 32) on a 32-bit build using `tar.NewReader`.

### What did you expect to see?
`tr.Next()` should return `ErrHeader` because the UID cannot be represented in the platform-native `int` field (`Header.Uid`).

### What did you see instead?
`mergePAX` in `src/archive/tar/reader.go` parses the value with `strconv.ParseInt(v, 10, 64)` and casts it directly to `int`:
```go
case paxUid:
    id64, err = strconv.ParseInt(v, 10, 64)
    hdr.Uid = int(id64)
```
On 32-bit systems where `sizeof(int) == 4`, `int(4294967296)` truncates to `0`. `tr.Next()` succeeds with `Header.Uid == 0` without reporting an error.

triage.title: x/net/quic: Initial packet padding can exceed anti-amplification limit
triage.body:
QUIC Initial packets sent by both the client and the server must be sent in a datagram which is padded to at least 1200 bytes.

The total amount of data sent by a server prior to confirming the client's address is restricted by the anti-amplification limit (3x the amount of data received from the client).

We aren't properly accounting Initial datagram padding against the anti-amplification limit, which permits a server to send data in excess of the limit under some circumstances.

This was reported to us as a potential security issue. The x/net/quic package is experimental, and the bar for considering a bug in it to be a security issue is quite high. Even if it were not experimental, we'd probably consider this a non-security bug, since the practical impact is low.

Regardless, this is a bug worth fixing.

triage.title: net/http, x/net/http2: HTTP/2 IDNA processing skips validation
triage.body:
The HTTP/2 transport converts the target hostname of a request to ASCII via simple Punycode translation without most validation. (It incorrectly uses idna.ToASCII instead of idna.Lookup.ToASCII) This permits invalid results, such as translating the Unicode name "a⒈com" ("a\u2488com") to the ASCII hostname "xn--acom-0w1b".

This affects direct use of `"golang.org/x/net/http2".Transport.RoundTrip` with pre-1.27 Go versions, and direct use of `"golang.org/x/net/http2".Transport.NewClientConn` with all Go versions.

This does not affect use of HTTP/2 via net/http, except for a corner case where a request for the ASCII version of the invalid name which succeeds can be followed by a request for the Unicode version which may reuse the cached connection from the prior attempt.

The practical impact of this is that under some scenarios, fetching a URL with a hostname containing non-ASCII characters can result in a request being sent to the Punycode-translated ASCII host.

This was reported to us as a potential vulnerability. We don't see a good way to exploit this.

It permits a request to "g\u200bo.dev" (non-breaking space, renders as "go.dev") to be sent to "xn--go-g1t.com", which is potentially surprising but TR #46 validation is not really intended to prevent confusables of this nature.

It does not permit a request to "xn-go-.dev" to be rewritten to "go.dev", since idna.ToASCII (after the fix for #78760) rejects xn- labels encoding ASCII-only strings.

Still a bug worth fixing.

triage.title: cmd/compile: omit or normalize line numbers in export data (.x) for incremental build pruning
triage.body:
### Background & Motivation

Build systems that split `cmd/compile` outputs into a small export data file (`-o pkg.x`, containing `__.PKGDEF`) for downstream `compile` actions and a full linker object (`-linkobj pkg.a`, containing `_go_.o`) for `link` actions can skip recompiling reverse dependencies when `pkg.x` is unchanged.

However, because Unified IR encodes source line/column numbers (`src.Pos`) and internal linker symbol indices into `__.PKGDEF`, internal edits to a source file—such as adding comments, blank lines, or unexported functions above an exported declaration—shift line numbers and change `pkg.x`. When a core library with many reverse dependencies is edited, this forces all downstream packages to recompile even when the exported API and inlineable function bodies are unchanged.

### Discussion Context from CL 837805

In [CL 837805](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/837805), we proposed a `-nolinenum` flag in `cmd/compile` that omits line numbers (and unexported symbol indices) from `.x` export data while preserving full source positions in the package's own `_go_.o` (`.a`) archive.

In the review discussion on [CL 837805](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/837805), it was noted that because export data includes the bodies of functions that can be inlined across packages, omitting line numbers from `.x` causes cross-package inlined frames in stack backtraces to lose their inner line numbers.

We'd like to discuss whether there is an approach here that would be acceptable to the Go toolchain—for example, explicitly indicating in stack traces/diagnostics when a line number was omitted due to `-nolinenum`, or another way to stabilize `.x` export data across line shifts without degrading stack backtraces.

triage.title: runtime/pprof: support dynamic languages with "virtual frames"
triage.body:
Several interpreters for dynamic languages are implemented in Go, such as [starlark-go](https://pkg.go.dev/go.starlark.net/starlark), [go-lua](https://github.com/Shopify/go-lua), [ivy](https://github.com/robpike/ivy), [goawk](https://github.com/benhoyt/goawk), and [many others](https://awesome-go.com/embeddable-scripting-languages/). In all such projects, there comes a time when the users start to ask for profiling tools. The interpreter maintainer has essentially no way to build high-quality implementations of these tools, because (a) they require direct integration into the runtime and so cannot be implemented in application code, and (b) a profile of an interpreter is an inextricable mix of operations in two languages--host (Go) and target--so a profile of just the target language is incomplete.

Fortunately the Go runtime/pprof package provides high-quality implementations of profilers for many resources including CPU, allocation, and so on. This proposal seeks to open them up to support dynamic languages.

The basic problem is that profiling an interpreter produces a profile that attributes much of the the resource cost of each target language function to the interpreter's general "eval" function, which is implemented in Go, when the user really wants to know which target language function is being evaluated. The solution (or vague outline of a solution) we propose here is a mechanism to allow applications to register with the runtime certain "eval" functions, marking them as special, so that when the profiler's stack unwinder encounters them, it should instead report a "virtual frame" whose (function name, file name, line number) triple is provided by the interpreter.

For this to work, there needs to be a local variable (or perhaps multiple variables) inside the eval function from which the triple can be derived, and the unwinder needs to be able to find it reliably, even in a handler for an async signal such as SIGPROF. This means the compiler must be instru

triage.title: runtime/metrics: add metrics for gauges of number of goroutines by stack size
triage.body:
I've been working on getting our memory usage down in a bunch of our servers. Once I got rid of a bunch of the useless heap retention, I set my sights on stacks and (re-)learning how Go stack growth and shrinking works.

One of the things that's been useful is we modified our Go fork to give us stats about the current goroutine's stack size (https://github.com/tailscale/go/commit/7b6f1558e73b1b5be03374b65687836ff9322e90 (same license as Go itself, CLA on file) so we can then have, with a little tracker helper that calls `runtime.TailscaleReadStackStats(m *TailscaleStackStats`), Prometheus metrics showing a breakdown of number of goroutines by size:

e.g. from one of our staging servers:

```
# TYPE blocked_stack_sizes gauge
blocked_stack_sizes{size="16384"} 50
blocked_stack_sizes{size="32768"} 6
blocked_stack_sizes{size="8192"} 0
```

But that helper requires us to explicitly add track points just before we expect to be blocked for long periods of time.

It'd be nicer if the `runtime/metrics` kept those stats for us all the time.

`GODEBUG=traceallocfree=1` is the closest thing we have today, but is pretty heavy for what I'd like.

To be clear, I'm not proposing adding our `runtime.TailscaleReadStackStats`. That was just a painless way to get approximately what we want with minimal runtime changes.

Thoughts?

triage.title: x/tools/gopls: add CodeLens for implementation counts on interfaces
triage.body:
`gopls` supports `textDocument/implementation` for Go interfaces, but it does not currently expose implementation counts through CodeLens.

This means editors that rely on server-provided CodeLens data cannot show a common IDE affordance such as:

```go
type Reader interface { // 3 implementations
	Read([]byte) (int, error)
}
```

This would be useful for quickly discovering interface usage and navigating large codebases without explicitly invoking "Go to Implementation" first.

A possible design is to add an optional CodeLens source for Go files, for example:

```json
{
  "codelenses": {
    "implementation": true
  }
}
```

The source could annotate non-empty interface type declarations with 1 implementation / N implementations.

To avoid making textDocument/codeLens expensive, the initial request could only scan the current file for candidate interface declarations and return unresolved CodeLens items. The implementation count could then be computed lazily through codeLens/resolve, reusing the existing implementation query machinery.

For navigation, the resolved CodeLens could use the existing gopls.lsp command to issue a standard textDocument/implementation request. Clients that support handling command results may present the returned locations using their normal implementation UI; clients that do not would still benefit from the implementation count.

triage.title: proposal: cmd/go: add go test -fuzztimereset option
triage.body:
### Go version

go version go1.25.x linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
Not available at the moment. I can provide the full `go env` output later if needed.
```

### What did you do?

### What version of Go are you using?

go version go1.25.x

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes.

### What did you do?

The built-in Go fuzzer currently supports stopping after a fixed duration using `-fuzztime`.

In practice, during long-running fuzzing campaigns, coverage often reaches a plateau long before the configured timeout expires.

For example:

- coverage grows during the first several minutes;
- afterwards no new interesting inputs or coverage are found for tens of minutes or even hours;
- the fuzzer continues consuming CPU until `-fuzztime` expires.

This is especially noticeable in CI and Kubernetes-based fuzzing infrastructure where CPU time is limited.

This is not a new fuzzing concept. AFL++ provides a similar mechanism through the `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME` environment variable:

> `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME` causes afl-fuzz to terminate if no new paths were found within a specified period of time (in seconds). May be convenient for some types of automated jobs.

Reference:
https://aflplus.plus/docs/env_variables/#settings-for-afl-fuzz

### What did you expect to see?

It would be useful to have a stopping condition based on coverage progress rather than only elapsed time.

For example:

```text
go test -fuzz=FuzzFoo -fuzzplateau=10m
```

where the fuzzer exits if no new coverage has been discovered for 10 minutes.

Alternatively, exposing coverage progress or "new coverage discovered" events through an API or statistics would allow external orchestrators to implement their own stopping policy without introducing a new command-line flag.

### What did you see instead?

Currently the only built-in stopping condition is elapsed time (`-fuzztime`), so fuzzing continues even when coverage has not changed for a long period.

triage.title: x/tools/go/analysis/passes: analyzer for removing canonical import comments
triage.body:
In module mode, since Go 1.11, `// import "..."` [comments on package declarations](https://go.dev/doc/go1.4#canonicalimports) are silently ignored by the toolchain. They are dead [documentation noise](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/26367#issuecomment-405666468). I propose adding an analyzer that removes such comments.

**Before**:

```go
package pdf // import "rsc.io/pdf"
```
or
```go
package pdf /* import "rsc.io/pdf" */
```

**After**:

```go
package pdf
```

triage.title: x/build: publish periodic tip binary builds for CI tooling
triage.body:
It would be useful for the Go project to publish periodic binary builds of Go tip, so CI tooling can make testing against a recent development version of Go as easy as:

```yaml
- uses: actions/setup-go@vN
  with:
    go-version: tip
```

The main motivation is to make it easier for Go package maintainers to find compatibility problems before a major Go release ships. Today, projects that want early signal can use `golang.org/dl/gotip`, which is very flexible: it can build the latest commit, a specific older commit on the main branch, a development branch, or even a CL still in review.

However, `gotip` works by downloading source and building Go. For many GitHub Actions users, that is enough friction that they do not add tip testing to their CI matrix. Pre-built tip archives would make the common case much easier: “test against a reasonably recent Go development build and report failures as non-fatal signal.”

There is related interest on the `actions/setup-go` side: https://github.com/actions/setup-go/issues/21. That action can already install released Go versions from binary archives, but supporting `go-version: tip` well likely needs an upstream source of official or semi-official tip build artifacts and machine-readable metadata.

There was prior discussion of nightly or periodic pre-release builds in #29205. At the time, one blocker was that the Go release process was still too manual. Since then, much of that automation work has landed, which may make periodic tip binary builds more feasible now.

This issue is not necessarily asking for a formal proposal immediately. Since this is mostly in `x/build` / release infrastructure territory, it may be enough to discuss the shape here first and promote it later only if needed.

triage.title: govulncheck-action: add allow-file input to risk-accept reachable advisories with no fix
triage.body:
### Proposal

Add an optional `allow-file` input to `golang/govulncheck-action`: a path to a file listing accepted advisory IDs (one `GO-YYYY-NNNN` per line; `#` comments and blank lines ignored). When set, the action runs govulncheck in JSON mode and fails only on reachable ("called") advisories whose ID is **not** listed. When empty (the default), behavior is unchanged — any reachable advisory fails the run.

### Motivation

The action's default text-mode gate fails on **any** reachable advisory, with no in-workflow override. govulncheck's call-graph reachability already excludes imported-but-unreachable advisories, but some **reachable** advisories have **no upstream fix** (`Fixed in: N/A`) — e.g. a CLI/client that links a server-side symbol transitively via `k8s.io/kubernetes` or `github.com/docker/docker`. There's no module to bump and no call to drop, so the gate blocks the consumer's builds indefinitely through no fault of the change.

The only current recourse is to stop using the action and hand-roll an equivalent JSON-mode + allowlist step. An `allow-file` input keeps the gate strict by default while allowing explicit, reviewed, version-controlled risk acceptance.

This is the action-level analogue of #61211 (silencing findings in govulncheck itself). An action input is useful today and would compose with native tool-level silencing later.

### Proposed interface

```yaml
- uses: golang/govulncheck-action@v1
  with:
    go-version-file: go.mod
    allow-file: .govulncheck-allow.txt   # default '' (strict)
```

- Empty / unset (default): unchanged — any reachable advisory fails.
- Set: JSON-mode scan; fail only on reachable advisories not listed. A missing file is treated as an empty allowlist (strict).

### Reference implementation

Backward-compatible (default empty = current behavior): https://github.com/devantler/govulncheck-action/tree/feat/allow-file — classifies reachable findings via `trace[0].function` and fails on the non-allowlisted set. Happy to

triage.title: cmd/go: go mod tidy can automatically maintain toolchain directive when godebug default requires a higher toolchain
triage.body:
This is a minor friction report and a suggested feature request to address it, similar to #74739, except it's about the `godebug` directive and its default key.

Consider a module with a `go 1.25.0` directive. If a `godebug default` directive is added with something higher than go1.25.0, then that becomes the minimum toolchain when working inside the module. It'd be good if the go command noticed that and automatically maintained the `toolchain` directive. As is, it leaves the module in a state where if an older go toolchain is used, it fails to parse the go.mod file:

```
$ GOTOOLCHAIN=local go version
go version go1.25.0 darwin/arm64
$ cd $(mktemp -d)
$ go mod init test
$ go get go@1.25.0
$ go mod edit -godebug default=go1.26.0
$ go mod tidy
$ go list -m
go: error loading go.mod:
go.mod:5: default=go1.26.0 too new (toolchain is go1.25.0)
```

If `go mod tidy` were to add a `toolchain go1.26.0`, then `go list -m` could succeed via the usual https://go.dev/doc/toolchain mechanism:

```
$ go list -m
go: downloading go1.26.0 (darwin/arm64)
test
```

The workaround for now is to manually maintain the `toolchain` directive (as was done in [CL 772660](https://go.dev/cl/772660) for example).

CC @golang/command-line.

```
for i := len(arr) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {

to

triage.title: cmd/compile: bounds check elision cannot reason through non-dominating blocks
triage.body:
Consider the following program:

```go
//go:nosplit
func use(z, x []int) int {
    if len(x) == 0 {
        return 0
    } else if len(x) > cap(z) {
        z = make([]int, len(x))
    } else {
        z = z[:len(x)]
    }
    return z[len(x)-1]
}
```

There is no input which can make it panic, but it emits a bounds check for `z[len(x)-1]`, despite `len(z) == len(x) > 0`:

```s
        TEXT    .use(SB), NOSPLIT|ABIInternal, $64-48
        PUSHQ   BP
        MOVQ    SP, BP
        SUBQ    $56, SP
        MOVQ    AX, 72(FP)
        MOVQ    DI, 96(FP)
        TESTQ   SI, SI
        JEQ     pc112
        CMPQ    CX, SI
        JGE     pc87
        NOP
        CMPQ    SI, $4
        JHI    pc59
        LEAQ    24(SP), CX
        MOVUPS  X15, (CX)
        MOVUPS  X15, 16(CX)
        LEAQ    24(SP), AX
        JMP     pc87
pc59:
        MOVQ    SI, 104(SP)
        LEAQ    type:int(SB), AX
        MOVQ    SI, BX
        MOVQ    BX, CX
        CALL    runtime.makeslice(SB)
        MOVQ    104(SP), SI
pc87:
        LEAQ    -1(SI), CX
        NOP
        CMPQ    SI, CX
        JLS     pc120
        MOVQ    -8(AX)(SI*8), AX
        ADDQ    $56, SP
        POPQ    BP
        RET
pc112:
        XORL    AX, AX
        ADDQ    $56, SP
        POPQ    BP
        RET
pc120:
        CALL    runtime.panicBounds(SB)
```

After much poking at the structure of this code, I've concluded that the issue is the fact that the bounds information comes from non-dominating blocks which collectively dominate the load. This is unfortunate, because this notably affects `math/big.nat.make`, which wants to be `append(z[:0], make(nat, n))`, but in the case where `n <= cap(z)` results in a redundant call to memclr. This has the knock-on effect that other code in math/big needs to (redundantly) teach the optimizer about bounds checks in the "usual way".

Maybe I'm getting something wrong here, but it looks like a genuine missed optimization to me.

triage.title: x/tools/gopls: detect and recover from snapshot/disk incoherence
triage.body:
A snapshot caches the content of every file it has read, to keep derived calculations such as type-checked packages coherent. But `go list` reads disk, not the cache, so the two can diverge whenever a closed file changes on disk without a corresponding `didChangeWatchedFiles` event. #64235 is one symptom ([repro and mechanism](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/64235#issuecomment-4277552611)); #63822 is probably another.

In other words, we hold every workspace file in memory to defend against incoherence, and it isn't sufficient: with the current go command APIs there is no way to guarantee that `go list` and gopls observe the same file state. We should stop paying the memory cost for a guarantee we don't get, and instead make incoherence recoverable.

Concretely:
- **Detect the inconsistency** by checking for inconsistent metadata from `Load`, or unexpected file content changes. It would be nice if the `go` command returned a manifest of file identities for files it read.
- **Recover** by recreating the view from scratch; we've so heavily optimized start up time so that this should be possible.
- **Degrade gracefully** by making most things work when gopls is initializing or reinitializing (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/69523) -- I'm doing this.
- **Alert the user**. Mechanism T.B.D., a "reinitializing" progress at least, but maybe also a popup warning of incoherent disk state.
- **Drop file contents** 🥳 

Alternatives:
- copy all the files to a temp directory and run go list there (this is effectively like passing a full overlay). 🤮

triage.title: x/tools/gopls: mcp: support a single shared daemon across all projects (multi-workspace MCP)
triage.body:
## Background

`gopls mcp` initializes its LSP session by calling `os.Getwd()` at startup and locking that directory as the workspace root for its entire lifetime. This is correct for single-project use, but means that a shared daemon cannot serve agents working in different projects — each would get analysis results rooted at the wrong module.

Today's workaround: per-project daemons (one per `(binary, workdir)` pair), as implemented in the community proxy [gopls-mcp-proxy](https://github.com/Afterous/gopls-mcp-proxy) and proposed for `-remote=auto` in #75270.

## Proposal

Support a **single gopls MCP daemon per machine** (keyed on binary only, like the existing LSP `-remote=auto` daemon) that can serve MCP clients across multiple projects simultaneously.

This is a parity gap: the LSP daemon already does this today. `gopls -remote=auto` starts a single machine-wide process that manages multiple workspace views across projects. This proposal brings `gopls mcp` to the same level.

This requires gopls to dynamically load workspace views when a new MCP client connects from a project not yet known to the daemon.

## What's Missing

The MCP roots mechanism already exists: when a client connects and sends `notifications/roots/list_changed`, gopls receives the client's workspace roots via the `watchRoots` callback (`cmd/mcp.go:160`). Currently this only starts file watching (`filewatcher.WatchDir`) but does **not** open a new LSP workspace view for that root.

The missing piece: when `watchRoots` fires with a root that isn't covered by any existing view, gopls should call the equivalent of `DidChangeWorkspaceFolders` on its internal server to open a new view for that module. The LSP server already supports dynamic workspace folder changes — this is about wiring MCP client roots into that mechanism.

## Relationship to #75270

	return x & (x | y) // should simplify to: return x
}

	return x | (x & y) // should simplify to: return x
}
```

### What operating system and processor architecture are you using?

triage.title: x/crypto/ssh: support parallel signing using request pipelining in ssh-agent
triage.body:
Hi, we're using the ssh-agent protocol as a way to access signing hardware such as yubihsms and tkeys. These devices have rather limited performance, so we're considering using multiple devices (configured with same keying material) to scale up performance.

The typical usage of the ssh-agent protocol is occasional interactive use, where a process like ssh connects, sends a few requests, typically including at most one signing request, and disconnects. Our use is rather different, with a long lived connection, and potentially several signing requests per second, with signing rate ideally limited only by the available signing hardware.

To use several devices in parallel, we'd update our agents to do request pipelining, i.e., read the next request and start processing it (load-balancing on available devices), before replying to the previous request. The ssh agent protocol supports this usage, as long as responses are sent in the correct order. 

However, if the agent client uses the x/crypto/ssh/agent package, it can't take any advantage of an agent doing signing operations in parallel, since the way it works (which is totally fine for the more traditional usecases) is that it locks the connection mutex, sends a requests, and blocks waiting for the response. See https://cs.opensource.google/go/x/crypto/+/refs/tags/v0.49.0:ssh/agent/client.go;l=342

It would be nice if the client could be extended to support request pipelining, i.e., as soon as a request is successfully put onto the wire (or more typically, into some unix socket buffer in the kernel) to the agent, be ready to send next request, and at at the same time, receive responses as they appear in order and return the result to the right caller. I think such behavior could be enabled unconditionally with no api changes, or there could be some configuration knob for the client, to limit the number of outstanding requests.

For more context, see also https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/issues/66

@FiloSottil

triage.title: cmd/compile: calling a method causes interface with non-pointer receiver to escape
triage.body:
Consider the following program:

```go
package p

type k int

func (k) F() {}

type y interface {
    F()
}

func f(k k)  {
    sink(k)
}

//go:noinline
func sink(v y) {
    v.F()
}
```

Here is `f`'s assembly:

```
TEXT    .f(SB), ABIInternal, $24-8
        PUSHQ   BP
        MOVQ    SP, BP
        SUBQ    $16, SP
        CALL    runtime.convT64(SB)
        MOVQ    AX, BX
        LEAQ    go:.k,.y(SB), AX
        NOP
        CALL    .sink(SB)
        ADDQ    $16, SP
        POPQ    BP
        RET
```

Notice that the argument is heap-allocated by calling `runtime.convT64`. If I remove the interface call in the method, the interface value does not escape and lives on the heap instead.

I think that what's happening here is that because for a general interface, calling an interface method can cause the receiver to escape, the escape bits are populated as such in the middle-end. However, the caller knows the interface's value, and if it knew that escape depends on the interface's methods escaping their first argument, it would know that the interface cannot escape.

This is a limitation in how escape information is recorded across function calls; there is no way to record "arg `n` escapes only if function pointer arg `m`'s `k`th argument escapes".

It is a little bit annoying on my end... I don't have a (painless) workaround for this in one of my APIs, but it actually does impact performance. I don't expect this to get fixed any time soon, because it requires a bit of a data model enhancement in the escape bits.

triage.title: simd/archsimd: AVX instructions do not make use of memory operands
triage.body:
Consider the following program (https://godbolt.org/z/fYxz6E86j):

```go
package p

import "simd/archsimd"

// Imagine this is filled with fun stuff.
var masks [16][16]int8

func f(v archsimd.Int8x16, n int) archsimd.Int8x16 {
    return v.Add(archsimd.LoadInt8x16(&masks[n&0xf]))
}
```

This generates this assembly:
```s
        TEXT    command-line-arguments.f(SB)
        ANDL    $15, AX
        SHLQ    $4, AX
        LEAQ    command-line-arguments.masks(SB), CX
        ADDQ    CX, AX
        VMOVDQU (AX), X1
        VPADDB  X1, X0, X0
        RET
```

Compare what LLVM generates for equivalent LLVM IR (https://godbolt.org/z/5a3YWdPja):

```ll
@g = external global <16 x i8>

define <16 x i8> @f(<16 x i8> %v, i64 %i) {
    %q = getelementptr <16 x i8>, ptr @g, i64 %i
    %w = load <16 x i8>, ptr %q
    %u = add <16 x i8> %v, %w
    ret <16 x i8> %u
}
```

This produces (forcing AVX support with -mcpu):

```s
f:
        mov     rax, qword ptr [rip + g@GOTPCREL]
        shl     rdi, 4
        vpaddb  xmm0, xmm0, xmmword ptr [rax + rdi]
        ret
```

Go's codegen is suboptimal for a few reasons:

1. Increased register pressure; 15 is surprisingly few vector registers, so generating memory ops is pretty important.
2. Worse code density --  I have not yet checked if this has actual icache consequences, but I would be surprised if both produce the same RISC86 on Zen3+.

IME, I trust LLVM's isel better than I trust myself to interpret AMD's optimization manual, so that's probably a good benchmark to check against for selection decisions.

triage.title: x/sys/unix: add Readv, Writev, Preadv, Pwritev for OpenBSD
triage.body:
## Problem

`readv(2)`, `writev(2)`, `preadv(2)`, and `pwritev(2)` are supported in
`golang.org/x/sys/unix` for Darwin, Linux, and Illumos, but not for OpenBSD.

OpenBSD 7.5+ forbids direct syscalls via `syscall.Syscall(SYS_*)` — all calls
must go through libc trampolines. Because `unix.Readv` does not exist for
OpenBSD, downstream Go programs that need vectored reads have no native API.
The only workaround is a sequential loop of `syscall.Read` calls in userspace.

A concrete example: xray-core uses `readv(2)` for efficient TCP buffer reads
(`common/buf/readv_posix.go`). On OpenBSD 7.5+ this silently returns EAGAIN on
non-blocking sockets even when data is present, causing connections to hang
with no logged error. See: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/3291

## Background: why direct syscalls are forbidden on OpenBSD 7.5+

OpenBSD implemented a syscall pinning mechanism (`pinsyscall(2)`) described by
[Theo de Raadt in December 2023 (openbsd-tech mailing list)](https://marc.info/?l=openbsd-tech&m=170205367232026&w=2).

The kernel now maintains a per-process table of exactly which syscall
instructions are permitted and from which addresses inside libc.so. Any syscall
instruction executed outside those registered locations is rejected.

This is intentional security hardening — not a bug. Go's runtime historically
bypassed libc entirely, emitting `SYSCALL` instructions directly. That approach
is now incompatible with OpenBSD 7.5+. The Go team already addressed this for
the most common syscalls by routing them through libc trampolines
(`syscall_openbsd_libc.go`). The vectored I/O syscalls simply haven't been
added yet.

## Current state

`SYS_READV = 120` and `SYS_WRITEV = 121` constants already exist in all 7
`zsysnum_openbsd_*.go` files. `read` and `write` are already implemented via
libc trampolines in `syscall_openbsd.go`:

```
//sys	read(fd int, p []byte) (n int, err error)
//sys	write(fd int, p []byte) (n int, err error)
```

triage.title: runtime: degraded performance on multi-NUMA-node machines
triage.body:
This performance bug can be seen in the latest Golang today on specific (common) current hardware.

Currently, Golang's global free list is not segregated into NUMA nodes. Work stealing also not NUMA-node aware. 

A **2x penalty** in memory accesses  can be seen on NUMA-node misses ([ref](https://codemia.io/blog/path/NUMA-Is-the-New-Network-How-Per-Socket-Memory-Models-Are-Reshaping-Microservice-Placement?utm_source=chatgpt.com)). Today, AMD EPYC exposes 4 NUMA nodes. Modern chiplet economics suggest NUMA is a growing trend.

Go could either (or some mix of):
- Do nothing, forcing devs into the penalty (as I'm seeing today on a specialty cloud deployment),
- Recommend CGroups to lock a process to CPUs or NUMA nodes (sounds awful to use and not cross-platform),
- Segregate operations & work-stealing completely (could starve unnecessarily & run-up free-list size),
- Prefer its NUMA node, but fallback to using others for free-list & work-stealing, 
- Use some more clever "cross-NUMA sometimes" logic, or
- Expose it to the developer somehow: today's `LockOSThread()` doesn't apply to `new()`.

Allocations in the free. list can come from anywhere. Even if new() was NUMA-specific, once a GoRoutine is stolen across NUMA zones, not-only will most of its previous RAM accesses get 2x slower, but new allocations give it no particular "home NUMA" node, which can create a piece of hot code that is working between 2 different NUMA nodes. If GoRoutines have a "home P" then memory could be allocated there and it could be returned there once stolen & paused in the hopes that it will generally stay in that node. 

Ultimately, Go cannot protect developers from the experience of this bottleneck as I can trivially create 2 big lists on different 'P' and diff them in a way that gets me crossing the NUMA boundaries. triage.title: x/text/encoding/charmap: add support for codepage ibm-273 or ibm-1141
triage.body:
IBM code page 273 (or update 1141 with Euro € sign) is an EBCDIC code page with the full [Latin-1 character set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8859-1) (ISO/IEC 8859-1) used on IBM mainframes in Austria, Germany.

It would be great if charmap could support a conversion from and to [ibm-273_P100-1999.ucm](https://github.com/unicode-org/icu-data/blob/main/charset/data/ucm/ibm-273_P100-1999.ucm) or the successor [ibm-1141_P100-1997.ucm](https://github.com/unicode-org/icu-data/blob/main/charset/data/ucm/ibm-1141_P100-1997.ucm).

triage.title: x/build/cmd/relui: automate process of updating security tracking issues once release is complete
triage.body:
When doing a security release which contains PRIVATE track issues, we create placeholder security issues in the issue tracker. These issues are referenced in the release announcement, and are updated post-release to contain the release note, and are used to track when we submit the security patches to the public main branch.

Likely, we'll want to wait to do this until after #76157 is complete, since the metadata will contain all the necessary information to understand which issue to update (and the content to populate it with).

In theory, we can already extract this information from the release notes (which include the GitHub issue number), but this seems significantly more fragile.

CC @golang/release

triage.title: x/build/cmd/relui: automate process of upstreaming private-track security CLs on release day (for the main branch)
triage.body:
One of the things left out of initial scope of #77214 was:

> upstreaming to main branch - this has a lot in common to release branches, but we don't have an existing ref for this and there are more considerations for how to handle potential merge conflicts. This makes for a good followup.

Filing this issue to track that followup.

In terms of ordering, we have some flexibility here, but it might make sense to sequence this after:

- security metadata (tracked in issue #76157)
   - this can help get to the original security fix CLs that were rebased against the main branch and so should have less of a chance of merge conflicts
- combined monthly release workflow (next minor(s) + next RC)
   - this creates a natural place in the relui workflow to handle yet another release-adjacent set of steps, not related to any one release kind in particular

CC @golang/release.

triage.title: x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize: remove the fmtappendf modernizer
triage.body:
(I couldn't locate much previous discussion about this analyzer, so if this has been discussed already or if this isn't the best place to bring this up, feel free to close it.)

I tried applying the fmtappendf modernizer on a large codebase. After analyzing the changes, I concluded that it wasn't an obvious improvement overall and that we shouldn't use it. Based on this experience, and the assumption that it is fairly representative of the changes that this modernizer will accomplish on other codebases, I propose that we remove this modernizer. (My comments below also suggest some ways we might make the modernizer a lot smarter instead, but I'm not sure how difficult that might be.)

---

The first and biggest issue that I see is that for more than half of the sites where this modernizer adds `fmt.Appendf` calls, there is a much better code change to be made by taking into account a slightly larger bit of surrounding context.

A typical one is something like this:

``` go
func handleRoute(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	// ...
	w.Write([]byte(fmt.Sprintf("hello, %s!", name)))
}
```

fmtappendf turns it into:

``` go
w.Write(fmt.Appendf(nil, "hello, %s!", name))
```

but the better change would be:


``` go
fmt.Fprintf(w, "hello, %s!", name)
```

Another type of change that pops up a fair amount is where the expression is inside an `append` already:

``` go
append(constructByteSlice(), []byte(fmt.Sprintf("format str %d", xyz))...)
```

fmtappendf turns it into:

``` go
append(constructByteSlice(), fmt.Appendf(nil, "format str %d", xyz)...)
```

but the better version would be:


``` go
fmt.Appendf(constructByteSlice(), "format str %d", xyz)
```

---

The second issue is that it's not clear to me that the change is a Pareto improvement, even in the other cases where the surrounding context doesn't suggest a different, better change. Consider:

``` go
k := []byte(fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", name, id))
```

which becomes


``` go
k := fmt.Appendf(nil, "%s:%d", name

triage.title: proxy.golang.org: cross-origin requests blocked by Goa
triage.body:
I am building a client-side viewer for source in the Go Modules Proxy that uses Range requests.

Thankfully, the proxy explicitly allows CORS!

```
$ http https://proxy.golang.org/filippo.io/age/@v/v1.3.1.zip
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
...
```

Except it doesn't actually work from the browser, because Goa is enforcing a strict Fetch metadata based policy.

```
$ http https://proxy.golang.org/filippo.io/age/@v/v1.3.1.zip sec-fetch-site:cross-site sec-fetch-mode:cors sec-fetch-dest:empty
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=2592000,h3-29=":443"; ma=2592000
Content-Length: 1449
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: script-src 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-src 'none'; report-uri https://csp.withgoogle.com/csp/goa-fa2dfb7c_2
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Date: Sun, 08 Feb 2026 14:37:02 GMT
Vary: Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Dest
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
X-Goa-Security-Debug: cross-origin request blocked by Goa's sandboxed serving (see go/goa-http-serving#sandboxing for more information)
X-Xss-Protection: 0
```

This feels unintentional, could it be disabled?

While at it, can we add the following two headers to allow cross-origin Range requests?

```
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Range
Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Content-Range, Content-Length
```

Technically, the first needs to be sent in response to the pre-flight OPTIONS request, and the second in response to the actual GET, but it's fine to just send them both for OPTIONS and GET.

/cc @golang/tools-team

triage.title: net: improve handling of socket completion notification modes on Windows
triage.body:
I/O operations on sockets are currently optimized by calling [SetFileCompletionNotificationModes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-setfilecompletionnotificationmodes) with `FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS` and `FILE_SKIP_SET_EVENT_ON_HANDLE` unless Windows has a non-IFS services provider, in which case it is not safe to use `FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS` as per this [doc](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/troubleshoot/windows/win32/setfilecompletionnotificationmodes-causes-io-completion).

We should do a better job here:

- `FILE_SKIP_SET_EVENT_ON_HANDLE` is always safe to apply
- `FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS` can still be set in the presence of the offending providers if the socket is not owned by that provider.

triage.title: cmd/compile: emit better code for bit vectors
triage.body:
The core of a bit-vector lookup is often of this form:
```go
func f(table *[32]byte, x byte) bool {
	return table[x/8]&(1<<(x%8)) != 0
}
```
The compiler generates code such as the following, with a byte load followed by AND+SHL+TEST:
```
TESTB	AL, (AX)
MOVL	BX, CX
SHRB	$3, BL
MOVBLZX	BL, DX
MOVBLZX	(AX)(DX*1), DX
ANDL	$7, CX
MOVL	$1, BX
SHLL	CX, BX
TESTB	BL, DL
SETNE	AL
```
amd64 machines have a dedicated [BT instruction](https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/bt) which could replace the AND+SHL+TEST with a single-cycle ALU op. Could we add a pattern to the code generator to match it?

There's not much we can do to analogously improve the equivalent arm64 code, but there is a redundant zero-extend instruction that add a data dependency:
```
MOVB	(R0), R27
PCDATA	$0, $-1
UBFX	$3, R1, $5, R2
MOVBU	(R0)(R2), R2
AND	$7, R1, R1
MOVD	$1, R3
LSL	R1, R3, R1
AND	R2, R1, R1
MOVBU	R1, R1         // redundant
CMPW	$0, R1
CSET	NE, R0
```

triage.title: x/tools/gopls: modernizer for Go 1.19 atomic types (atomic.Int32, ...)
triage.body:
Go 1.19 introduced new atomic types (wrappers). Allowing one to replace:

```go
var x int32
for range 100 {
  go atomic.AddInt32(&x, 1)
}
```

With:

```go
var x atomic.Int32
for range 100 {
  go x.Add(1)
}
```

On the whole, this is safer, as the atomic types don't allow non-atomic access, which is a source of bugs. Note the `+checkatomic` annotation of [checklocks](https://pkg.go.dev/gvisor.dev/gvisor/tools/checklocks).

These new-style atomics also don't suffer from misalignment problems, see https://github.com/dominikh/go-tools/issues/171.

Not all usages are (easily) migratable, a non-exhaustive list of the top of my head:

 - Initialized values (e.g.: `x  := int32(42) `), though this could be done with an ugly closure, it may not be worth it.
 - Multi-package usages (exposed atomics, if they exist for some reason)
 - ...(probably a lot more)

cc @adonovan

triage.title: cmd/compile: optimize string concatenation to avoid runtime calls
triage.body: Hi team, I've identified a potential optimization opportunity to eliminate concat calls for constant strings and replace them directly with a LEAQ straddr instruction, similar to what the [Java JIT](https://github.com/openjdk/jdk/blob/master/src/hotspot/share/opto/stringopts.hpp) does. This is a cheap optimization that can enable further optimizations down the line, such as compile-time evaluation of len(const_string). A local run of .`/make.bash` shows 200+ potential sites for this optimization. Here is an example: ```go func ff(a, b int) string { y := "abc" t := y + "def" if t == "abcdef" { return t + "ghi" } return t } ``` before: after applying opts: For implementation, we could either - add a dedicated [stringopt pass](https://github.com/y1yang0/go/commit/2f74a406d7ff72255a995b6120129ffc26c735af) before expand_call (which centralizes the code for future optimizations like strcmp) or - integrate it into the [sccp pass](https://github.com/y1yang0/go/commit/d08577e5aa5185831715c19473fab49f57a0488d) after expand_call (which uses its framework but disperses the code) or - add some generic rules Do you have a preference on the approach? Would the community be interested in this?

triage.title: x/tools/gopls: add a way to export gopls metrics/logs
triage.body:
The old `-ocagent` option that let us export `gopls` metrics/logs to third-party data storage was removed in [CL 653016](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/tools/+/653016).

We actually had a wrapper for `gopls` that ran an HTTP server to receive this data and forward it to our internal storage. We had to delete this wrapper when the `-ocagent` flag was removed. At the time, it wasn't a huge deal since we didn't have the resources to build proper dashboards anyway.

I'm now getting back into monitoring, and we have a number of developers complaining that "gopls doesn't work." It would be extremely useful to have these data available again to properly debug and track the service.

Can we implement a (similar) way to export metrics/logs from `gopls` without patching its code?

I see there are some Prometheus counters, but they don't provide enough details, e.q duration of operations. Maybe we can extend Prometheus implementation?

triage.title: x/tools/gopls: when editing Go files in GOMODCACHE, offer to clone module and add replace directive
triage.body:
Being able to quickly edit the standard library (e.g. by inserting a print statement) is extremely useful during debugging. However, editing source files from dependencies within the module cache is not as convenient. Gopls could detect an attempt to modify such a file and offer to clone the module, add a [replace directive](https://go.dev/ref/mod#go-mod-file-replace) to the main module, and move the cursor to the corresponding position in the cloned file, which can then be freely edited. triage.title: go/types: infer generic type when it can be inferred without ambiguity
triage.body:
```
func dummyGeneric[E any](input, input2 E) E {
	return input
}

func dummyString(input, input2 string) string {
	return input
}

func _() {
	x := dummyGeneric("") // missing input 2
	y := dummyString("") // missing input 2

	x = "" // type of x is invalid
	y = "" // type of y is string
}
```

In the code snippet above, both the function call miss one input parameter. The type checker successfully figured out the type of `y` is string because it is not a generic function. However, the type checker did not successfully figured out the type of `x` is `string`. 

When developing gopls, we encounter a lot of cases where the go source file is broken especially when the user is typing. A good use case is auto-completion in a generic function call

```
var x []string
slices.ContainsFunc(x, ${cursor})
```

In snippet above, the cursor is in the position of the second input parameter. It is clear that the user want to type `func(s string) bool {}`. But because we can not infer the generic type, we can not offer such auto-completion.


This is a FR to ask if type checker could infer the generic type if the context provide an un-ambiguous resolution. The type checker should keep the generic type invalid if the context is confusing

```
func foo[E any](input1, input2, input3 E) {}

func _() {
    foo("", "", ${type}) // the type is string
    foo("", 1, ${type}) // the type is invalid
}
```

We could try to match the argument to the signature by it's order. But I'm proposing the matching mechanism simply because it is the simplest and it matches the most with the human behavior. (as we tend to write input parameter from left to right.)
```
Signature (arg0, arg1, arg2, arg3 ....)
           /       /      /
Call (input0, input1, input2 ...)

Signature (arg0, arg1, arg2, arg3 ....)
           /       /      /
Call (input0, ${miss}, input2 ...)
```

cc @adonovan  @mrkfrmn

triage.title: Fuzzing test plus extracting regexp definition of time.ParseDuration
triage.body:
This is a small proposal (that I intend to implement if accepted)

The method time.ParseDuration has a [comment right after start](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.25.5:src/time/format.go;l=1622) of a regexp that presents which strings are parsable by it.

My proposal is to:
- Mention it in documentation
- Probably expose it as a **nonexported** constant of the package - this way it can be used in fuzzying directly without parsing the code (otherwise I will just parse the code)
- Document that it is not normative, source code remains the source of truth
- Create a [fuzz test](https://go.dev/doc/security/fuzz) to show that it is equivalent to the source code

Pluses:
- A real example of fuzz test used within the go toolchain
- In case no new dependencies are allowed - I can do simple fuzzying without resorting to the the oss-fuzz library
- Simple documentation of what other languages/frameworks can expect time.ParseDuration to take
- Easy check that the doc string is in sync with the implementation

Minuses:
- In case the implementation of parse.Duration is changed - the regexp may need to be changed. However this is the case even now. 

Outside the proposal:
- I am not proposing changing the implementation
- I am not proposing using regex-es as substitute 
- I am not proposing exposing the regex outside the package
- I am not proposing making the regex normative

What I expect is answer whether this is a good idea and has some chance of being accepted.
I will then propose some patches.
If it will definitely be not accepted - just say so and close the issue.
